The page claims that the quality of e-Lecture material on many pages has reached the lecture standard of NUS algorithm classes. For logged-in NUS students, VisuAlgo can load according to their class setup and saved preferences.

For verified non-NUS computer science lecturers, account-specific functionality includes access to hidden slides containing answers to questions on preceding visible slides.

**Online Quiz system**

Each visualization module includes its own online quiz. The quiz system provides:

- A built-in question generator
- Randomly generated questions based on specific rules
- A built-in answer verifier
- Submission to a grading server
- Almost-instant automatic grading

The public can access quizzes through **Training mode**. The page distinguishes this from **Test mode**, which provides a more controlled environment for randomly generated questions and automatic verification in official NUS examinations.

The page does not contain scripted fixed question text. Instead, questions are generated by the system and submitted for automatic evaluation. More questions are being added to the question bank.

Verified computer science lecturers can access the **Hard** setting. For NUS, quizzes can carry a small but non-zero assessment weight if instructors use them in their courses. The page argues that repeated practice with automatically verifiable questions can improve basic concept mastery and reduce manual basic-question load in examinations.

**Accounts and stored preferences**

Global account registration opened in June 2023 and is no longer limited to addresses associated with NUS. A visitor can use the login page and follow its on-screen instructions to create an account.

A general account can store settings such as:

- Layout mode
- Default language
- Playback speed
- Other customization settings

Account categories include:

- **NUS students:** used for course-specific visualization/e-Lecture setup, progress tracking, and official quizzes
- **NUS official accounts:** identified using an NUS official email address, the student’s name as listed in the class roster, and an encrypted password
- **Non-NUS computer science lecturers:** identified using a non-NUS email, any display name, and an encrypted password; these accounts distinguish instructor credentials from public access

Users may delete their own accounts. NUS accounts are normally purged after the associated course unless the user opts in to retaining the account.

**NUS course tracking**

With a VisuAlgo account, an NUS student consents to having the course lecturer track:

- Reading progress through e-Lecture slides
- Online quiz training progress

The stated purpose is to support smooth operation of the course. An NUS VisuAlgo account is required for official NUS online quizzes. Sharing account credentials with another person so that they can take a quiz on the student’s behalf is described as an academic offense.

Only the three required account elements are said to be stored: official NUS email, class-roster student name, and a server-encrypted password. Access to the full database, including encrypted passwords, is restricted to Prof. Halim himself.

**Internationalization and translation**

VisuAlgo is presented as a trilingual platform with routes for:

- English: `/en`
- Chinese: `/zh`
- Indonesian: `/id`

The site provides translation statistics and aims for nearly 100% translation in all three languages. The extracted text also states that Chinese and Indonesian translations are currently behind and therefore redirect visitors to English.

The project has public explanatory notes in:

- Indonesian
- Korean
- Vietnamese
- Thai

Only translators with at least 100 translations are counted in the contributor statistics.

**Performance and caching**

VisuAlgo uses Cloudflare’s global CDN, which is intended to provide fast first loads. The page claims that returning visits load “almost instantly” because large quantities of static VisuAlgo content are cached.

Users are advised not to use incognito or private-browsing mode if they want the cache retained. Normal account login may also cause the site to load a preferred or course-specific configuration.

**Desktop and mobile use**

The original visualizations were not designed for small touch screens because intricate graphics need substantial pixel space and click-and-drag interaction. The recommended minimum resolution is:

\[
1366 \times 768
\]

Since April 2022, a mobile “lite” version has been available. It supports a subset of VisuAlgo functionality on smartphones, but the page makes clear that the full experience is intended for larger screens.

**Languages, APIs, and installation**

No programming-language API, function signature, package installation command, or local setup procedure is provided on this page. The only programming-language reference is that recursive functions visualized by the site must be expressible in JavaScript.

The service is accessed through `VisuAlgo.net`; no installation is required for the online version. Personal offline use of client-side files is allowed, but the online quiz depends substantially on server-side scripts and databases.

**Privacy**

The privacy section is version 1.2, updated on 18 August 2023. Since that date:

- Google Analytics is no longer used.
- Cookies are used only for the operation of VisuAlgo.
- The cookie-consent popup is disabled, including for first-time visitors.

For ordinary global users, an account consists of the relevant email address, display name where applicable, and an encrypted password. Lecturer status is used to provide instructor-oriented features, including hidden answer slides and access to the Hard quiz setting.

**Project history and contributors**

Associate Professor Steven Halim has served as project leader and adviser from July 2011 onward. Dr. Felix Halim, identified as a senior software engineer at Google, is also listed in the project history.

Student contributions were organized through several periods of undergraduate research and final-year/UROP projects, spanning 2011 through 2025. These included:

- Undergraduate Student Researchers 1
- Final Year Project/UROP students 1
- Undergraduate Student Researchers 2
- Final Year Project/UROP students 2
- Undergraduate Student Researchers 3
- Final Year Project/UROP students 3
- Optiver-associated researchers in 2023

The NUS Centre for Development of Teaching and Learning granted a Teaching Enhancement Grant to start the project. Optiver funding began in August 2023, with the stated funding period running from mid-2023 to mid-2026 and potentially beyond.

A planned 2026 expansion would investigate new information-visualization techniques, potentially including AI-assisted methods. This is described as a future focus, not a currently implemented feature.

**Terms of use**

VisuAlgo is offered at no cost to the global computer science community. Students and instructors may use it directly in their classes.

Users may share the site through:

- Facebook
- YouTube
- Instagram
- TikTok
- Twitter
- Course webpages
- Blog reviews
- Email

Screenshots and videos may be reused elsewhere if the user cites:

- `https://visualgo.net`
- And/or the listed publications

The following restrictions apply:

- Client-side files may not be downloaded and hosted on another website.
- Forking the project is not permitted.
- Creating VisuAlgo variants is not permitted.
- Personal offline use of the client-side application is acceptable.

The quiz system has a substantial server-side component, so its scripts and databases are not easy to reproduce locally. Public users access quizzes through training mode. Test mode is reserved for a more controlled environment used by NUS.

**Publications and continuing development**

The system was presented at:

- The CLI Workshop during ICPC World Finals 2012 in Warsaw, Poland
- The IOI Conference at IOI 2012 in Sirmione-Montichiari, Italy

The page links to a 2012 paper describing the predecessor system, which was not yet named VisuAlgo, and a 2015 short update linking the previous project name with VisuAlgo.

The page explicitly describes VisuAlgo as unfinished. Bugs in visualization pages or the online quiz system, and requests for new features, are directed to Associate Professor Steven Halim.

## Key Concepts & References

- **VisuAlgo** — interactive visualization and e-learning platform for data structures and algorithms
- **Steven Halim** — project leader, adviser, and NUS School of Computing associate professor
- **Felix Halim** — project contributor and co-author of *Competitive Programming*
- **Suhendry Effendy** — co-author of *Competitive Programming*
- **Competitive Programming** — source book for numerous advanced algorithms represented in VisuAlgo
- **DFS/BFS** — depth-first and breadth-first graph traversal visualization
- **MST** — minimum spanning tree visualization
- **SSSP** — single-source shortest-path visualization
- **Kruskal’s algorithm and Prim’s algorithm** — example algorithms for side-by-side comparison
- **Binary Max Heap**
  - Binary Tree representation
  - Compact Array representation
- **Linked lists**
  - Manual `/list` layout
  - Emphasis on the near-\(O(1)\) behavior of most operations
- **Recursion trees**
  - JavaScript recursive functions
  - DAG representations for overlapping dynamic-programming subproblems
- **Online Quiz**
  - Random question generation
  - Automatic answer verification
  - Training mode
  - NUS test mode
  - Hard lecturer setting
- **e-Lecture Mode** — integrated explanatory slides and notes
- **Graph DS, Max Flow, Matching, MVC, Steiner Tree, and TSP** — explicitly named graph-related modules
- **Cloudflare global CDN** — first-load delivery infrastructure
- **NUS CDTL** — provided the initial Teaching Enhancement Grant
- **Optiver** — project funder from 2023, with planned support through mid-2026 and possibly beyond
- **2012 CLI Workshop at ICPC World Finals**
- **2012 IOI Conference**
- **2015 VisuAlgo name/project update**

## Takeaways

- VisuAlgo is a free, browser-based learning platform that combines custom-input algorithm animation, e-Lecture explanations, and automatically graded quizzes.
- Its defining strength is that learners can test their own data and compare related visualizations rather than only follow fixed examples.
- The platform currently has 24 visualization modules; the page explicitly identifies nine graph modules but does not enumerate all 24.
- e-Lecture Mode, user accounts, saved preferences, and course-specific loading support both self-paced learning and classroom use.
- Training quizzes are publicly accessible, while test mode and selected instructor capabilities are controlled.
- Full use is best on larger screens; a subset of features is available through the mobile “lite” version.
- Reuse of screenshots or videos is allowed with attribution, but redistribution, cloning, and creation of variants are prohibited.
- VisuAlgo remains under active development, with future work exploring additional information-visualization methods, potentially with AI assistance.

resources.title: Data Structures and Algorithms Course in Hindi
resources.summary:
## Overview

This is a Hindi-language, beginner-to-intermediate Data Structures and Algorithms course focused on placement preparation, interviews, and logic building. The 92-video playlist is organized as a progression from algorithm analysis and linear structures to trees, graphs, sorting, searching, and spanning trees, with many implementations written in C. Concepts are presented through explanations, examples, operation walkthroughs, complexity analysis, and coding sessions.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

### 1. Data Structures, Algorithms, and Complexity Analysis

- Importance of data structures and algorithms in solving real-world problems efficiently.
- Introduction to common data structures such as arrays, stacks, and linked lists.
- Asymptotic time-complexity analysis.
- Big O notation.
- Big Omega notation.
- Big Theta notation.
- Best-case, worst-case, and average-case analysis of algorithms.
- Solving time-complexity problems.
- Practical calculation of Big O for programs and algorithms.
- Comparing algorithmic performance using asymptotic analysis.

### 2. Arrays and Array ADT

- Arrays as a fundamental data structure.
- Abstract Data Type (ADT) representation of arrays.
- Why arrays are needed.
- Advantages and disadvantages of array storage.
- Implementing an array as an ADT.
- Implementing array operations in C.
- Array traversal.
- Array insertion.
- Array deletion.
- Array searching.
- Coding array insertion in C.
- Coding array deletion in C.
- Linear search.
- Binary search.
- Comparing linear and binary search.
- Coding linear and binary search in C.
- Linear search complexity: `O(n)`.
- Binary search complexity: `O(log n)`.

### 3. Linked Lists

- Introduction to linked lists.
- Motivation and benefits of linked lists.
- Comparison of linked-list organization with arrays.
- Creating a singly linked list in C.
- Traversing a linked list.
- Inserting a node into a singly linked list.
- Insertion at the beginning, middle, or end of a linked list.
- Deleting a linked-list node.
- Deleting from the beginning, end, a specified position, or by key.
- C implementation of linked-list deletion.
- Circular linked lists.
- Traversing and displaying circular linked lists.
- Circular-linked-list operations in C.
- Doubly linked lists.
- Displaying and traversing doubly linked lists in C.
- Forward and backward links in doubly linked-list representations.

### 4. Stacks and Stack Applications

- Introduction to the stack data structure.
- Stack as a linear data structure.
- Stack access order and top-based operations.
- Implementing a stack using an array.
- C implementation of an array-based stack.
- `push()` operation.
- `pop()` operation.
- `isEmpty()` operation.
- `isFull()` operation.
- `peek()` operation.
- `stackTop()` operation.
- `stackBottom()` operation.
- Time-complexity analysis of stack operations.
- Implementing a stack using a linked list.
- Using the linked-list head pointer as the stack top.
- C implementation of linked-list-based stack operations.
- `peek()`, `stackTop()`, and related linked-list stack operations.
- Parentheses matching using a stack.
- Checking balanced parentheses in C.
- Matching multiple types of parentheses.
- Valid-parentheses problem as a stack application.
- Infix expressions.
- Prefix expressions.
- Postfix expressions.
- Relationship between infix, prefix, and postfix notation.
- Infix-to-postfix conversion using a stack.
- Coding infix-to-postfix conversion in C.
- Expression evaluation context for stack-based algorithms.

### 5. Queues and Deques

- Introduction to the queue data structure.
- Queue as a linear structure.
- FIFO ordering: first-in, first-out.
- Enqueue operation.
- Dequeue operation.
- Different ends for insertion and removal.
- Implementing a queue using an array.
- Queue-array state variables and movement of front/rear positions.
- C implementation of array-based queue operations.
- Queue `isFull()` and `isEmpty()` operations.
- Introduction to circular queues.
- Space wastage in ordinary array-based queues.
- Circular queue wraparound.
- Circular increment of queue pointers.
- Circular-queue `enqueue()` and `dequeue()`.
- Other circular-queue operations.
- C implementation of circular queues.
- Implementing a queue using a linked list.
- Front and rear pointers for linked-list queues.
- C implementation of linked-list-based queues.
- Double-Ended Queue (Deque).
- Front and rear ends of a deque.
- Operations at both ends of a deque.

### 6. Sorting Algorithms

- Need for sorting algorithms.
- Real-world uses of sorting.
- Criteria for analyzing sorting algorithms.
- Performance analysis of sorting algorithms.
- Bubble Sort.
- Bubble Sort process and implementation in C.
- Insertion Sort.
- Insertion Sort process and implementation in C.
- Selection Sort.
- Selection Sort comparisons and swaps.
- Selection Sort implementation in C.
- Selection Sort as a non-adaptive algorithm.
- Selection Sort as a non-stable algorithm.
- QuickSort.
- Partitioning in QuickSort.
- Recursive QuickSort organization.
- QuickSort analogy and step-by-step example.
- QuickSort implementation in C.
- Best-case, worst-case, and average-case analysis of QuickSort.
- Merge Sort.
- Merging two sorted arrays.
- Recursive sorting in Merge Sort.
- Merge Sort implementation in C.
- Counting Sort.
- Counting objects with distinct key values.
- Counting Sort implementation in C.

### 7. Trees and Binary Trees

- Introduction to tree data structures.
- Tree terminology.
- Root.
- Children.
- Siblings.
- Parent.
- Leaf node.
- Internal node.
- External node.
- Depth.
- Height.
- Introduction to binary trees.
- Definition of a binary tree.
- At most two children per node.
- Left child and right child.
- Recursive binary-tree representation using a root and left/right subtrees.
- Full or strict binary tree.
- Perfect binary tree.
- Complete binary tree.
- Degenerate or pathological tree.
- Skewed binary tree.
- Balanced binary tree.
- Array representation of binary trees.
- Pointer or linked representation of binary trees.
- Linked binary-tree representation in C.
- Preorder traversal.
- Inorder traversal.
- Postorder traversal.
- C implementation of preorder traversal.
- C implementation of postorder traversal.
- C implementation of inorder traversal.
- A shortcut or trick for finding preorder, inorder, and postorder traversals of large trees.

### 8. Binary Search Trees and AVL Trees

- Introduction to Binary Search Trees (BSTs).
- BST as an ordered or sorted binary tree.
- Keys larger than a node in its left subtree.
- Keys smaller than a node in its right subtree.
- Checking whether a binary tree satisfies the BST property.
- Searching in a binary search tree.
- Recursive or basic BST search strategy.
- C implementation of BST search.
- Iterative search in a BST.
- Insertion in a BST.
- BST insertion strategy.
- Deletion in a BST.
- Cases involved in BST deletion.
- C implementation of BST deletion.
- Introduction to AVL trees.
- Need for AVL trees instead of ordinary BSTs in some situations.
- Insertion in an AVL tree.
- Rotation in an AVL tree.
- Left-Left (LL) rotation.
- Left-Right (LR) rotation.
- Right-Left (RL) rotation.
- Right-Right (RR) rotation.
- AVL insertion and rotation for small trees.
- Generalization of AVL rotation to trees with multiple nodes.
- C implementation of AVL insertion and LL, RR, LR, and RL rotations.

### 9. Graphs and Graph Traversal

- Introduction to graph data structures.
- Graphs as models of important real-world problems.
- Graph terminology and representation.
- Adjacency list representation.
- Adjacency matrix representation.
- Other graph representations.
- Graph traversal or graph search.
- Visiting, checking, or updating each vertex during traversal.
- Classification of graph traversals by visiting order.
- Tree traversal as a special case of graph traversal.
- Breadth-First Search (BFS).
- BFS traversal order.
- BFS spanning tree.
- Use of a queue to implement BFS.
- C implementation of BFS.
- Depth-First Search (DFS).
- DFS traversal order.
- C implementation of DFS.

### 10. Spanning Trees and Minimum Spanning Trees

- Spanning trees.
- Number of possible spanning trees in complete graphs.
- Calculating spanning-tree cost.
- Minimum Spanning Tree (MST).
- Prim’s algorithm.
- Prim’s algorithm as a greedy algorithm.
- Prim’s algorithm for weighted undirected graphs.
- Step-by-step Prim’s algorithm examples.

## Detailed Notes

### Data Structures, Algorithms, and Complexity Analysis

- The course begins by motivating why data structures such as arrays, stacks, and linked lists are important and why algorithms must be chosen for efficient real-world solutions.
- The analysis phase establishes time complexity as a way to describe how algorithm execution time grows with input size.
- Asymptotic notation is used instead of exact operation counts because the course focuses on growth behavior.
- The three principal notations introduced are:
  - **Big O**: upper-bound asymptotic analysis.
  - **Big Omega**: lower-bound asymptotic analysis.
  - **Big Theta**: tight asymptotic bound.
- The playlist explicitly covers best-case, worst-case, and average-case analysis. The learner is expected to identify which case applies to a particular input or execution path.
- Time-complexity calculation is treated as a skill: the course includes solved questions and walks through calculating Big O for algorithms and programs.
- A central habit is to reason about how the size of the input affects the number of operations rather than focusing only on a program’s running time for one small input.

### Arrays

- Arrays are introduced as a basic linear data structure and then reconsidered as an Abstract Data Type, or ADT.
- The ADT treatment separates the array’s conceptual operations from its implementation details.
- The course discusses why arrays are useful, along with their advantages and disadvantages.
- The standard array operations covered are:
  - traversal,
  - insertion,
  - deletion,
  - and searching.
- Insertion and deletion are implemented in C, so the learner is expected to understand how an array’s contiguous structure affects these operations.
- The course compares two searching techniques:
  - **Linear search**: checks elements sequentially and runs in `O(n)`.
  - **Binary search**: uses the ordered structure of the array and runs in `O(log n)`.
- The videos include C code for both searching methods, making the course practical as well as conceptual.

### Linked Lists

- Linked lists are presented as an alternative to arrays and are motivated by their own benefits and organization.
- The course begins with the creation and traversal of a singly linked list in C.
- A node-based list is then used to study insertion. Insertion is considered at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end.
- Deletion is treated as a major linked-list operation. The course considers deletion from:
  - the beginning,
  - the end,
  - a specified position,
  - and a node identified by its key.
- Circular linked lists are introduced after ordinary singly linked-list operations. The playlist demonstrates how circular lists can be created, traversed, displayed, and implemented in C.
- Doubly linked lists are then introduced. Their distinguishing representation allows movement in both directions through the list, and the course demonstrates how to display and work with them in C.

### Stacks

- A stack is introduced as a linear data structure with a restricted access pattern centered on its top.
- The course covers the main stack operations:
  - `push()`,
  - `pop()`,
  - `peek()`,
  - `isEmpty()`,
  - `isFull()`,
  - `stackTop()`,
  - and `stackBottom()`.
- The array implementation is developed first, including the need to track the stack’s top and capacity-related state.
- The C implementation directly demonstrates `push()`, `pop()`, `isEmpty()`, and `isFull()`.
- `peek()` is then implemented separately, followed by access to the top and bottom positions.
- The time complexities of stack operations are explicitly considered.
- A second implementation uses a linked list. The key design idea is to use the linked-list head pointer as the stack top.
- This implementation includes `push`, `pop`, `isEmpty`, `peek`, and `stackTop`-style operations in C.

#### Parentheses Matching

- Parentheses matching is used to demonstrate why a stack is useful in computer systems.
- For the basic problem, opening parentheses are pushed and closing parentheses are matched against the stack’s most recent opening symbol.
- The C implementation checks whether an expression has balanced parentheses.
- The problem is then extended to multiple parenthesis types, where the closing symbol must match the corresponding opening type.

#### Infix, Prefix, and Postfix

- The course introduces infix, prefix, and postfix as different ways of writing arithmetic expressions.
- Infix-to-postfix conversion is implemented using a stack.
- The playlist includes both a manual procedure and a C program for the conversion.
- The stack is used while scanning the infix expression to produce the postfix form.
- The course places this conversion within the broader family of stack applications and expression-notation problems.

### Queues

- A queue is defined as a linear structure that follows FIFO order: the item stored first is accessed first.
- The insertion side is used for `enqueue`, while the opposite side is used for `dequeue`.
- The array implementation tracks the queue’s front and rear positions and includes the standard operations:
  - `enqueue()`,
  - `dequeue()`,
  - `isFull()`,
  - and `isEmpty()`.
- C code implements the array-based queue.
- The course then introduces circular queues to address space wastage in an ordinary array implementation.
- A circular queue advances pointers circularly: when a pointer reaches the end of the array, it returns to the beginning.
- The C implementation covers circular-queue enqueue, dequeue, and related operations.
- Linked-list queues are implemented with front and rear pointers.
- A Double-Ended Queue, or deque, is then introduced as a collection with both a front and a rear where items can remain positioned while operations are performed at its two ends.

### Sorting Algorithms

- The sorting section begins with the need to arrange data and the practical use of sorting in real applications.
- Students are shown how to analyze sorting algorithms by their performance criteria.
- The course then develops several sorting algorithms in order.

#### Bubble Sort

- Bubble Sort is described as a simple and well-known sorting algorithm.
- It is explained conceptually and then implemented in C.
- The implementation provides coding practice for the basic sorting process.

#### Insertion Sort

- Insertion Sort is explained using examples.
- The algorithm is then implemented in C so that the learner can connect the visual sorting process to source code.

#### Selection Sort

- Selection Sort is used to sort an array of size `n`.
- The course discusses the comparisons and swaps performed while reaching the final time complexity.
- Its C implementation is provided as a function that accepts an array and sorts it.
- Selection Sort is explicitly identified as a **non-adaptive** and **non-stable** sorting algorithm.

#### QuickSort

- QuickSort is explained using partitioning and a broader divide-and-conquer-style organization.
- The course uses an analogy to explain the algorithm and then develops its overall idea.
- The C implementation covers the QuickSort algorithm.
- A separate analysis lesson calculates the best-case, worst-case, and average-case behavior of QuickSort.

#### Merge Sort

- Merge Sort is introduced through the problem of merging two sorted arrays into one sorted array.
- Once the merge procedure is understood, the algorithm recursively sorts the entire array.
- The course then provides a deeper C implementation.

#### Counting Sort

- Counting Sort works by counting objects having distinct key values.
- The C implementation uses the counted key frequencies to construct the sorted result.

### Trees and Binary Trees

- A tree is introduced through terms such as root, children, siblings, parent, leaf node, internal node, external node, depth, and height.
- A binary tree is a tree in which each node has at most two children, designated as the left child and right child.
- A recursive definition represents a nonempty binary tree as a root together with left and right subtrees, either of which may be empty.
- The course distinguishes several binary-tree types:
  - **Full or strict binary tree**
  - **Perfect binary tree**
  - **Complete binary tree**
  - **Degenerate or pathological tree**
  - **Skewed binary tree**
  - **Balanced binary tree**
- Binary trees can be represented using arrays or pointers.
- The linked representation is studied in greater detail and coded in C.
- The three standard traversal orders are:
  - **Preorder**: visit the root before the subtrees.
  - **Inorder**: visit the left subtree, root, and right subtree.
  - **Postorder**: visit the subtrees before the root.
- Each traversal is implemented in C.
- The playlist also provides a shortcut or trick for finding preorder, inorder, and postorder traversals on large trees.

### Binary Search Trees

- A Binary Search Tree is a rooted binary tree with an ordering property: keys in a node’s left subtree are smaller, while keys in its right subtree are larger, as stated in the course description.
- The course first explains how to check whether a given binary tree satisfies the BST property.
- Searching follows the ordering of the tree rather than examining every node.
- Search is implemented in C and also presented in an iterative form.
- BST insertion places a new key by following the appropriate left or right path.
- Deletion is treated as a multi-case operation because the deleted node can be at different positions or can have children.
- The C implementation focuses on coding the deletion cases.

### AVL Trees

- AVL trees are introduced as a response to situations in which an ordinary binary search tree can become unbalanced.
- The course covers AVL insertion and the rotations needed after insertion.
- The four named rotation situations are:
  - **LL**
  - **LR**
  - **RL**
  - **RR**
- The lessons first demonstrate insertion and rotation on small trees, then extend the method to trees with multiple nodes.
- A final coding lesson implements AVL insertion and LL, RR, LR, and RL rotations in C.

### Graphs and Graph Traversal

- Graphs are introduced as important structures for modeling real-world problems.
- The playlist covers graph representation using:
  - adjacency lists,
  - adjacency matrices,
  - and other representations.
- Graph traversal, also called graph search, is the process of visiting each vertex, including checking or updating vertices.
- The visiting order determines the traversal classification.
- Tree traversal is identified as a special case of graph traversal.

#### Breadth-First Search

- BFS explores a graph level by level.
- The course discusses the BFS spanning tree.
- A queue is used to implement BFS because the vertices discovered at one level must be processed in breadth-first order.
- BFS is implemented in C.

#### Depth-First Search

- DFS explores as far as possible along the current path before returning to explore other paths.
- DFS is introduced as a graph traversal algorithm and implemented in C.

### Spanning Trees and Minimum Spanning Trees

- Spanning trees are introduced after graph traversal.
- The course considers the maximum number of possible spanning trees in complete graphs.
- Students are shown how to calculate the cost of a spanning tree.
- The minimum spanning tree is introduced as the key graph optimization object of the final section.
- Prim’s algorithm is presented step by step with examples.
- It is identified as a greedy algorithm for finding a minimum spanning tree in a weighted undirected graph.

## Key Formulas & Concepts

- **Data structure:** An organized way of storing and accessing data.
- **Algorithm:** A step-by-step method for solving a problem.
- **Abstract Data Type (ADT):** The conceptual interface and operations of a data structure, considered separately from its implementation.
- **Time complexity:** Growth rate of an algorithm’s execution time relative to input size.
- **Asymptotic notation:** Big O, Big Omega, and Big Theta.
- **Big O:** Upper-bound asymptotic analysis.
- **Big Omega:** Lower-bound asymptotic analysis.
- **Big Theta:** Tight asymptotic analysis.
- **Best case:** Analysis of the most favorable execution case.
- **Worst case:** Analysis of the most expensive execution case.
- **Average case:** Analysis based on expected or average input behavior.
- **Linear search complexity:** `O(n)`.
- **Binary search complexity:** `O(log n)`.
- **Array operations:** Traversal, insertion, deletion, and searching.
- **Singly linked list:** Nodes connected through one next link.
- **Circular linked list:** A linked list whose traversal wraps around.
- **Doubly linked list:** Nodes connected in both forward and backward directions.
- **Stack:** Linear structure organized around a top element.
- **Stack operations:** `push()`, `pop()`, `peek()`, `isEmpty()`, `isFull()`, `stackTop()`, and `stackBottom()`.
- **LIFO-style stack behavior:** The most recently pushed item is the first one removed.
- **Queue:** Linear structure following FIFO.
- **Queue operations:** `enqueue()` and `dequeue()`.
- **Circular queue:** Queue whose array positions wrap from the end back to the beginning.
- **Deque:** Double-ended queue with front and rear ends.
- **Infix notation:** `operand operator operand`.
- **Prefix notation:** `operator operand operand`.
- **Postfix notation:** `operand operand operator`.
- **Binary tree:** Tree in which each node has at most two children.
- **Preorder traversal:** Root, left subtree, right subtree.
- **Inorder traversal:** Left subtree, root, right subtree.
- **Postorder traversal:** Left subtree, right subtree, root.
- **Binary Search Tree:** Ordered binary tree based on left/right key relationships.
- **AVL tree:** Height-balanced BST maintained through rotations.
- **LL, LR, RL, RR:** Four AVL imbalance/rotation cases.
- **Graph traversal:** Process of visiting graph vertices in a defined order.
- **BFS:** Breadth-first graph traversal implemented with a queue.
- **DFS:** Depth-first graph traversal.
- **Spanning tree:** Tree used to connect the vertices of a graph.
- **Minimum Spanning Tree:** Spanning tree with minimum cost.
- **Prim’s algorithm:** Greedy algorithm for finding an MST in a weighted undirected graph.
- **Bubble Sort:** Simple sorting algorithm.
- **Insertion Sort:** Sorting algorithm developed through examples and C implementation.
- **Selection Sort:** Non-adaptive, non-stable sorting algorithm.
- **QuickSort:** Sorting algorithm based on partitioning and recursive organization.
- **Merge Sort:** Recursive sorting algorithm based on merging sorted arrays.
- **Counting Sort:** Sorting method based on counting objects with distinct key values.

## Takeaways

- The course provides a structured path from foundational algorithm analysis through arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, and graphs.
- C is the primary implementation language, so students should be able to translate data-structure operations and algorithms into working functions and programs.
- The learner must distinguish between algorithmic cases and asymptotic notations, especially when comparing `O(n)` and `O(log n)` searching.
- Stack and queue applications are emphasized

## Takeaways

- A2Z is a sequential DSA roadmap containing approximately 450 learning items, 400+ practice problems, and 50 theory lessons across 19 modules and 95 focused sections.
- No prior DSA knowledge is required, but basic familiarity with variables, loops, functions, arrays, strings, input/output, and debugging in one programming language is expected.
- The central learning method is to understand patterns, start with brute force, improve the solution, justify correctness, and analyze complexity before implementing independently.
- Concepts are taught language-independently and can be implemented in C++, Java, Python, JavaScript, Go, or C#.
- Timed practice, post-attempt solutions, editorials, contextual hints, code reviews, and revision tools support repeated engagement rather than solution memorization.
- The intended outcome is interview readiness: choosing data structures, optimizing approaches, coding under pressure, answering follow-up questions, and maintaining a revision system.

## Detailed Notes

### 1. Foundations and problem-solving style

The playlist starts with environment and language preparation before moving into algorithmic reasoning. VS Code setup and input/output formatting are treated as practical competitive-programming prerequisites. The C++ basics lesson supplies the only explicitly identified language-focused foundation in the playlist description, while the broader course is described as pseudocode-based. The complexity lesson establishes the need to evaluate both running time and memory use rather than treating a solution only as a sequence of steps.

The pattern lesson is explicitly framed as “22 Patterns in 1 Shot” and focuses on reusable construction techniques. The STL lesson is similarly broad: its title identifies a complete C++ STL overview, time complexity, and notes. For DSA work, these lessons provide the basic vocabulary for expressing algorithms, implementing containers, and reasoning about their costs.

The basic-math lesson introduces number-theoretic tools needed later. In particular, the Euclidean algorithm is the named technique for computing the greatest common divisor. The recursion sequence then moves from a conceptual introduction to progressively more structured forms:

1. recursion and recursion trees;
2. basic recursion problems;
3. parameterised recursion;
4. functional recursion;
5. problems involving multiple recursive calls.

Recursion trees are useful for visualizing how recursive calls expand. The playlist explicitly connects recursion with stack space, so a recursive solution must be analyzed not only by its branching factor and depth but also by the space occupied by active calls. Parameterised recursion passes state through arguments, whereas functional recursion receives and returns results from recursive calls. Multiple-call recursion is the basis for combining answers from independent subproblems and later becomes important in divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, graph traversal, and tree algorithms.

### 2. Hashing and sorting

The hashing lesson introduces maps, hash tables, time complexity, collisions, and the division rule of hashing. The division rule computes a hash location from the key and a chosen divisor; collisions occur when different keys map to the same location, so hashing must be analyzed together with collision handling and lookup behavior.

Sorting begins with three foundational comparison sorts:

- **Selection sort** repeatedly selects

## Detailed Notes

### Algorithms and computational problem solving

The central objective of the course is to turn a computational problem into an algorithm that can be shown to be both **correct** and **efficient**. Efficiency is not treated as an afterthought: algorithm choices are connected to mathematical models of computation, data structures, and asymptotic performance analysis.

A useful solution framework is:

1. Model the input and desired output.
2. Choose an appropriate computation model and data structure.
3. Design the algorithm.
4. Give a correctness argument.
5. Derive an asymptotic running-time bound.
6. Communicate both arguments clearly.

The course repeatedly uses recurrence solving, especially the Master Theorem, to analyze divide-and-conquer-style algorithms.

### Asymptotic behavior

Asymptotic analysis ignores constants and lower-order terms and describes how computational work grows with input size.

For \(f(n)\), \(g(n)\):

\[
T(n)=O(f(n))
\]

means \(T(n)\) grows no faster than a constant multiple of \(f(n)\) asymptotically.

\[
T(n)=\Omega(f(n))
\]

means \(T(n)\) grows at least as fast as a constant multiple of \(f(n)\).

\[
T(n)=\Theta(f(n))
\]

means \(T(n)\) is bounded above and below by constant multiples of \(f(n)\).

When analyzing a function, dominant terms determine its asymptotic behavior. For example, polynomial terms dominate lower-degree terms, and exponential terms dominate polynomial terms. Constant-factor improvements matter for implementation performance, but asymptotic analysis focuses on eventual growth.

### Recurrences and the Master Theorem

Many algorithms divide a problem into smaller subproblems, admit a recurrence such as

\[
T(n)=aT(n/b)+f(n),
\]

and are analyzed by identifying:

- \(a\): the number of recursive subproblems,
- \(n/b\): the size of each recursive subproblem,
- \(f(n)\): the nonrecursive work at the current level,
- \(n^{\log_b a}\): the recursive work’s characteristic growth rate.

The Master Theorem states, for a recurrence of this form:

1. If
   \[
   f(n)=O(n^{\log_b a-\varepsilon})
   \quad\text{for some }\varepsilon>0,
   \]
   then
   \[
   T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a}).
   \]

2. If
   \[
   f(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a}),
   \]
   then
   \[
   T(n)=\Theta(n^{\log_b a}\log n).
   \]

3. If
   \[
   f(n)=\Omega(n^{\log_b a+\varepsilon})
   \quad\text{for some }\varepsilon>0,
   \]
   and the usual regularity condition holds, then
   \[
   T(n)=\Theta(f(n)).
   \]

Study strategy: first identify \(a\), \(b\), and \(f(n)\); then compute \(n^{\log_b a}\); then compare \(f(n)\) with that quantity. The three cases are a useful quiz framework.

### Data structures, sequences, and sets

A data structure combines a way to store data with algorithms supporting operations on that data. The supported operations form an interface.

The two central interfaces emphasized in the course are:

- **Sequence interface:** ordered items, with operations such as accessing, searching, inserting, deleting, and—when supported—working from both ends.
- **Set interface:** a collection supporting membership, search, insertion, and deletion without relying on sequence order unless a sorted representation is deliberately chosen.

The interface affects the cost of operations. A sequence may support positional navigation or double-ended operations, while a set emphasizes membership and updates. Dynamic arrays provide a basic array-based sequence foundation.

### Sorted sets and sorting

A set stored in sorted key order supports faster search than an unsorted structure. Binary search repeatedly compares a target with the middle element and discards the half that cannot contain the target.

If a sorted array has length \(n\), binary search uses logarithmically many comparisons:

\[
\Theta(\log n).
\]

The course also emphasizes that efficient search and efficient construction are separate concerns. A structure can answer queries quickly only after data have been organized appropriately.

Sorting methods discussed include:

- **Insertion sort:** building a sorted array or supporting insertion into sorted order.
- **Selection sort:** repeatedly selecting the next item for an array.
- **Comparison-based sorting:** arranging keys through pairwise comparisons.
- **AVL sort:** obtaining sorted output from set operations on an AVL tree.
- **Heap sort:** using a binary heap’s priority-queue structure.

A comparison sorting decision tree with \(n!\) possible output permutations requires height at least

\[
\Omega(\log_2(n!))=\Omega(n\log n).
\]

This is the standard comparison-sorting lower bound. Non-comparison methods such as counting and radix sort can improve on it when the keys have suitable structure.

### Hashing

A hash table maps a key to an array location through a hash function:

\[
h(k)=\text{index associated with key }k.
\]

Hashing supports fast dynamic operations on stored data without requiring global sorted order. The lectures discuss hash functions, lookup and updates, expected performance, hashing bounds, and the contrast between hashing and comparison-based search.

Typical expected hash-table operation time is constant, \(\Theta(1)\), although the lecture emphasizes reasoning about assumptions and bounds rather than treating hashing as unconditional. Hash-table pictures are used in problem sessions to show how keys map to buckets or array positions.

Set-to-sequence reductions emphasize that the operation model affects which algorithms and lower bounds apply.

### Linear sorting

The course examines ways to sort faster than general comparison sorting by exploiting key structure.

- **Direct-access array sorting** places a key into an array position determined by its value.
- **Tuple sorting** treats each item as a tuple, such as a key together with associated information.
- **Counting sort** counts occurrences of keys and uses cumulative counts to determine positions.
- **Radix sort** processes digits or key components in a stable order.

For counting a key range of size \(k\), the relevant work depends on both the number of items and the key range. Radix sort processes key components in successive passes, so its cost combines the number of items, the number of passes, and the range handled by each pass.

The key idea is that a sorting lower bound based only on comparisons does not prevent linear-time sorting when the input has additional exploitable structure.

### Binary trees and subtree augmentation

Binary trees support hierarchical navigation. The course applies them to both sequence and set interfaces.

For sequence trees, storing **subtree sizes** makes rank and order-statistic navigation possible. If the size of the left subtree is known, a position can be compared with that count to decide whether to move left, move right, or select the current node.

Tree updates require maintaining the augmented information. This is a general pattern: store extra information in each node, update it after modifications, and use it to guide faster operations.

### AVL trees

An AVL tree is height-balanced. For every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by at most one:

\[
|h_{\text{left}}-h_{\text{right}}|\le 1.
\]

Height is augmented so that balance can be checked after an update. Insertion or deletion can cause an imbalance; rotations repair the structure.

The relevant operations are:

- **Single rotation:** used for one common form of imbalance.
- **Double rotation:** a rotation performed through an intermediate configuration.
- **Rebalancing:** restoring the AVL height condition after a modification.

The balance condition prevents trees from degenerating into long lists. AVL height grows logarithmically in the number of stored elements, giving logarithmic set and sequence operations. The course’s “next steps” lecture also discusses related research directions in origami and folding designs, illustrating how tree and recursive structures can arise far beyond conventional data structures.

### Binary heaps and priority queues

A priority queue exposes access to an item with highest priority rather than general positional access. A binary heap stores items in a complete binary-tree layout and maintains a heap-order condition: each parent has higher priority than its children.

The array representation supports navigation through parent and child positions. Heap operations support efficient extraction of the highest-priority item and updating priorities.

Heap sort uses the priority-queue interface to repeatedly extract the next item and obtain elements in sorted order. The lecture connects heap sort with selection sort, insertion sort, and AVL-tree sorting, emphasizing that different data structures lead to different implementations of the same broad task.

### Graphs and BFS

A graph is represented through vertices and edges. A graph representation records adjacency information, commonly through neighbor sets or adjacency structures.

BFS explores vertices in increasing distance from a starting vertex. It is appropriate for shortest paths in unweighted graphs because all edges have equal length. The traversal produces a shortest-path tree rooted at the start.

The course also introduces **full BFS**, which processes the graph more comprehensively rather than only answering a narrowly specified query. Graph radius and graph schematics appear in problem sessions, requiring students to reason from complete traversal information and distances.

### DFS, topological sorting, and cycles

Depth-first search follows a path as far as possible before backtracking. **Full DFS** records the complete traversal.

DFS supports:

- directed-graph exploration,
- topological sorting of a DAG,
- cycle detection,
- classification of graph structure.

A topological order lists vertices so that directed edges respect ordering constraints. Topological order is available for acyclic directed graphs and can be used to evaluate dependencies or process recursive subproblems in a valid order.

### Weighted graphs and shortest paths

In a weighted graph, each edge has a numeric weight, and the weight of a path is the sum of its edge weights. The shortest-path problem therefore minimizes total weight rather than number of edges.

The course distinguishes:

- **single-source shortest paths (SSSP):** find a distance from one source to all reachable vertices;
- **all-pairs shortest paths (APSP):** find distances between every pair of vertices.

Weighted graph radius and weighted ratios apply shortest-path information to global graph questions.

### Bellman–Ford

Bellman–Ford solves the single-source shortest-path problem in general weighted graphs, including graphs with negative edge weights.

Its central operation is edge relaxation: if an edge \((u,v)\) can improve the current distance to \(v\), update the distance and predecessor information. The process is repeated for up to \(|V|-1\) rounds.

Its structure makes correctness depend on progressively incorporating paths with increasing numbers of edges. After \(|V|-1\) rounds, shortest paths can be finalized if no negative cycle affects the source.

Bellman–Ford is also a canonical dynamic program: distances improve according to an acyclic ordering of path-edge counts, even though the original graph may contain cycles.

### Dijkstra’s algorithm

Dijkstra’s algorithm solves single-source shortest paths in graphs with nonnegative edge weights. It maintains tentative distance labels, repeatedly selects the unsettled vertex with the smallest tentative distance, and relaxes its outgoing edges.

The correctness argument relies on the fact that, with nonnegative edge weights, selecting the smallest tentative distance is safe: a path through some other unsettled vertex cannot later produce a smaller total distance.

The edge-weight restriction is essential. Negative edges invalidate the greedy selection step. The lecture includes a worked example of applying Dijkstra’s algorithm.

### APSP and Johnson’s algorithm

All-pairs shortest paths require distances for every source-destination pair. Johnson’s algorithm reweights a general weighted graph so that Dijkstra can be used.

Reweighting uses values from Bellman–Ford and changes edge weights so that reweighted paths have a convenient order. Dijkstra is then run for every vertex, and the original distances are recovered.

This combines the general-graph capability of Bellman–Ford with the efficient nonnegative-edge behavior of Dijkstra.

### Dynamic programming framework

Dynamic programming begins with a recursive solution. Its key steps are:

1. Define a subproblem precisely.
2. Identify its base cases.
3. Find all smaller subproblems on which it depends.
4. Combine their results.
5. Evaluate the subproblems in a dependency-respecting order.
6. Store only the necessary results.
7. Use parent pointers if the actual solution must be reconstructed.

A subproblem should contain all information needed to determine the answer to the larger problem. It should not be so broad that it recombines unrelated solved instances, nor so narrow that the larger problem cannot be expressed in terms of it.

**Subproblem constraints** restrict what state is allowed. **Subproblem expansion** determines how the recursive recurrence breaks the state into smaller states. Parent pointers record which choice produced an optimal result.

### Dynamic programming examples

- **Fibonacci:** avoid recursively recomputing the same Fibonacci values.
- **DAG shortest paths:** use a topological order rather than a general weighted-graph algorithm.
- **Bowling:** the relevant state includes cumulative frame information.
- **LCS:** a subproblem is determined by prefixes of the two sequences.
- **LIS:** maintain information for progressively larger prefix endpoints.
- **Coins:** a state captures the amount remaining or a bounded prefix of coin types.
- **Floyd–Warshall:** use vertex subsets or allowed intermediate vertices as the subproblem state.
- **Arithmetic parenthesization:** a subproblem is a contiguous interval of the expression.
- **Piano or guitar fingering:** states encode constraints along a sequence.
- **Rods:** a state records the allowable rod length.
- **Subset sum:** a state records which items or sum progress have been considered.

For Floyd–Warshall, the conceptual recurrence is

D^{(k)}[i,j]
=
\min\left(

resources.title: Main Page - Algorithms for Competitive Programming
resources.summary:
## Overview

**Algorithms for Competitive Programming**, also called **CP-Algorithms**, is a free, ad-free, volunteer-run project that translates and expands material originating from the E-Maxx algorithms archive. It is intended for competitive programmers, algorithm learners, contributors, and maintainers who want descriptions of algorithms and data structures, with compiled pages published at `https://cp-algorithms.com/`.

The page itself is primarily a project landing page rather than an algorithm article. It describes the project’s purpose, contribution options, associated websites and repositories, and a chronological changelog covering documentation features, navigation, metadata, search, and community infrastructure.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- Project mission:
  - Translating the E-Maxx algorithm and data-structure resource.
  - Extending existing articles with additional material.
  - Adding new articles to the collection.
- Intended audience:
  - Competitive programmers.
  - Readers seeking algorithm and data-structure descriptions.
  - Contributors who author or translate articles.
  - Maintainers responsible for navigation and site organization.
  - Users interested in sponsoring article bounties.
- Project access and distribution:
  - Main compiled website: `https://cp-algorithms.com/`.
  - Original reference resource: `https://e-maxx.ru/algo`.
  - GitHub Pages mirror: `https://gh.cp-algorithms.com/`.
  - Auxiliary competitive-programming library: `https://lib.cp-algorithms.com/`.
  - Source repository: `https://github.com/cp-algorithms/cp-algorithms`.
- Participation:
  - Becoming a contributor.
  - Contributing articles.
  - Sponsoring bounties for articles.
  - Supporting the project’s donation system.
  - Joining the project’s Discord server.
- Documentation-generation system:
  - Migration to the **MkDocs** site generator.
  - Use of the **Material for MkDocs** theme.
  - Configuration and maintenance of article structure in `navigation.md`.
  - Separate navigation page.
  - Content tabs and sidebar navigation.
- Search, display, and rendering:
  - Dark mode.
  - Improved search.
  - More stable rendering of mathematical formulas.
  - Copyable LaTeX source for formulas.
- Article discovery and metadata:
  - Full article list through the navigation page.
  - Tag system for articles.
  - Translation versus original-content tags.
  - Tag index with overall tag information.
  - `From: X` tags linking translated articles to their originals.
  - Automatic RSS feeds for new articles.
  - Automatic RSS feeds for article updates.
  - Last-commit date tracking.
  - Author-list tracking.
  - Contribution percentages.
  - Commit-history access.
- Documented article maintenance:
  - Major overhaul of the article on finding strongly connected components.
  - Building a condensation graph.
- Project chronology:
  - Repository and owning-organization renaming.
  - Recommendation to update local upstream links.
  - Addition of new maintainers.
  - Changelog of infrastructure and publishing changes from January 2022 through August 2025.
- Licensing/access model stated on the page:
  - Ad-free operation.
  - Volunteer maintenance.
  - Free access for everyone.

## Detailed Notes

### Project purpose and scope

The project’s stated goal is to translate the resource at:

`https://e-maxx.ru/algo`

That source provides descriptions of numerous algorithms and data structures, particularly those popular in competitive programming. CP-Algorithms is intended to do more than mirror or translate this material: the project also aims to improve the collected knowledge by:

- Extending existing articles.
- Adding articles that are not yet represented.
- Increasing the overall coverage of competitive-programming algorithms and data structures.

The page presents CP-Algorithms as a community-supported knowledge project. It is:

- Ad-free.
- Volunteer-run.
- Free for everyone.
- Open to article contributions.
- Dependent on sponsors for article bounties and ongoing support.

### Publication locations and associated resources

Compiled pages are published at:

`https://cp-algorithms.com/`

A GitHub Pages-based mirror is available at:

`https://gh.cp-algorithms.com/`

An auxiliary competitive-programming library is available at:

`https://lib.cp-algorithms.com/`

The source repository was moved to:

`https://github.com/cp-algorithms/cp-algorithms`

The October 2022 changelog entry says that both the repository name and its owning organizations were renamed. Users with local clones or local repositories that track the project as an upstream are advised to update their upstream links.

The full set of articles is exposed through the site’s **Navigation** page. The complete revision history is available through **Commit History**.

### Contribution and community support

Users can participate by:

- Contributing articles.
- Helping sponsor bounties associated with articles.
- Supporting the project’s donation system.
- Becoming a contributor.
- Joining the Discord server launched in August 2025.

The page asks readers to support the donation system so that the project can continue growing. The donation-system overhaul is recorded as an August 2025 update.

Three maintainers are explicitly welcomed in the changelog:

- `jxu`
- `mhayter`
- `kostero`

The welcome appears in the October 2024 update.

### MkDocs publishing system

In January 2022, the project switched to:

- **MkDocs** as its site generator.
- **Material for MkDocs** as its theme.

The changelog gives several motivations for this change:

1. A more modern visual appearance.
2. Additional site features.
3. Dark mode.
4. Better search.
5. Greater rendering stability for mathematical formulas.
6. Easier contribution workflows.

The site uses content tabs and sidebar navigation. The navigation was moved to a separate page.

When an article is created, moved, or otherwise reorganized, the page says that the structure should be adjusted in:

`navigation.md`

This file is therefore part of the project’s article-organization workflow.

### Formula handling

As of October 31, 2022, users can select and copy the LaTeX source code of formulas within articles.

This complements the earlier migration to MkDocs, which was intended to improve the stability of mathematical-formula rendering.

The landing page does not provide any algorithmic formulas itself; the only formula-related content is the site-wide LaTeX-copying feature and the rendered symbol `$\LaTeX$` in the changelog.

### Tags and translation provenance

Tags were enabled on June 8, 2022. Each article is now marked as either:

- Translated.
- Original.

Overall tag information is available through a tag index.

For a translated article, selecting a:

`From: X`

tag leads to the original article. This provides a direct provenance link between a translation and its source article.

### Article and contribution metadata

Beginning June 7, 2022, the project tracks:

- The date of the most recent commit for each page.
- The list of authors associated with the page.
- Each author’s contribution percentage.

Together, these features expose both the freshness of a page and the distribution of work among contributors.

### Feeds and update discovery

On June 26, 2023, the project added automatic RSS feeds for:

- New articles.
- Updates to existing articles.

Users can therefore monitor additions and revisions without manually checking every page.

### Named article overhaul

On July 16, 2024, the project completed a major overhaul of the article titled:

- **Finding strongly connected components**
- **Building condensation graph**

The landing page mentions this article but does not reproduce its graph-theory definitions, algorithms, implementation, complexity analysis, or code. Those details are outside the extracted text.

### Changelog chronology

#### August 2025

- Overhauled the CP-Algorithms donation system.
- Requested support to help the project grow.
- Launched a Discord server.

#### October 2024

- Welcomed new maintainers `jxu`, `mhayter`, and `kostero`.

#### October 15, 2024

- Published a GitHub Pages-based mirror at `https://gh.cp-algorithms.com/`.
- Made an auxiliary competitive-programming library available at `https://lib.cp-algorithms.com/`.

#### July 16, 2024

- Completed a major overhaul of the strongly connected components / condensation graph article.

#### June 26, 2023

- Added automatic RSS feeds for new articles.
- Added automatic RSS feeds for article updates.

#### December 20, 2022

- Renamed the repository and owning organizations.
- Moved the repository to `https://github.com/cp-algorithms/cp-algorithms`.
- Recommended updating upstream links in local repositories.

#### October 31, 2022

- Enabled selection and copying of LaTeX formula source.

#### June 8, 2022

- Enabled article tags.
- Distinguished translated and original articles.
- Added an overall tag index.
- Added `From: X` links from translated articles to their originals.

#### June 7, 2022

- Added per-page last-commit dates.
- Added author lists.
- Added author contribution percentages.

#### June 5, 2022

- Enabled content tabs.
- Enabled sidebar navigation.
- Moved navigation to a separate page.
- Established `navigation.md` as the file to update when articles are created, moved, or reorganized.

#### January 16, 2022

- Migrated to MkDocs.
- Adopted the Material for MkDocs theme.
- Introduced dark mode.
- Improved search.
- Improved formula-rendering stability.
- Made the site easier to contribute to.

### Limitations of the supplied page text

This resource is a project home page, not a substantive algorithm tutorial. The extracted text does **not** provide:

- A complete list of algorithms or data structures.
- Explanations of any algorithm or data structure.
- Algorithm pseudocode.
- Source-code implementations.
- Complexity analysis.
- Competitive-programming examples.
- Exercises or problem sets.

The “New articles” heading appears in the extracted text, but no individual new-article titles are present beneath it. The full article inventory must be obtained from the linked **Navigation** page rather than inferred from this page.

## Key Concepts & References

- **Algorithms for Competitive Programming / CP-Algorithms**
  - Main project: `https://cp-algorithms.com/`
- **E-Maxx algorithms archive**
  - Translation and expansion source: `https://e-maxx.ru/algo`
- **MkDocs**
  - Static-site generator adopted by the project.
- **Material for MkDocs**
  - Documentation theme used with MkDocs.
- **GitHub**
  - Hosts the project repository at `https://github.com/cp-algorithms/cp-algorithms`.
- **GitHub Pages mirror**
  - Available at `https://gh.cp-algorithms.com/`
- **CP-Algorithms library**
  - Auxiliary library at `https://lib.cp-algorithms.com/`
- **Navigation page**
  - Provides the full article list and site structure.
- **`navigation.md`**
  - Site-structure file that should be updated when articles are created or moved.
- **Tag index**
  - Central index for translated/original article tags.
- **RSS feeds**
  - Automatic feeds for new articles and updates.
- **Finding strongly connected components / Building condensation graph**
  - Article receiving a major overhaul in July 2024.
- **Discord**
  - Community server launched in August 2025.
- **Article bounties**
  - Articles for which users can help obtain sponsorship.

## Takeaways

- CP-Algorithms is a free, ad-free, volunteer-run translation and extension of the E-Maxx competitive-programming archive.
- The main collection is at `https://cp-algorithms.com/`, with a GitHub Pages mirror and a separate auxiliary library.
- The project covers competitive-programming algorithms and data structures, but this extracted page functions only as a project landing page and changelog.
- The site is generated with MkDocs and the Material for MkDocs theme, providing features such as dark mode, improved search, and more reliable mathematical rendering.
- Article organization is maintained through a separate navigation page and the `navigation.md` structure file.
- Articles carry translation/original tags, provenance links, last-commit dates, author lists, and contribution percentages.
- RSS feeds provide automatic updates for new and revised articles, while contributors can help through article submissions, bounties, donations, or Discord participation.
