- General “best practices for prompt engineering” blog post.
- Interactive prompt engineering tutorial for Claude 3 models.
- Interactive spreadsheet tutorial.
- Model-specific tuning guidance for Claude’s latest models.

## Takeaways

- Define success criteria and build empirical evaluations before trying to optimize a prompt.
- Prompt engineering is most appropriate for outcomes that can be controlled by changing the prompt.
- Latency and cost problems may be better solved by selecting a different model.
- Claude’s “Prompting best practices” reference covers clarity, examples, XML structure, roles, thinking, and prompt chaining.
- Use the Claude Cookbook metaprompt recipe when no initial prompt exists.
- The interactive fundamentals tutorial targets Claude 3 models, so current best practices take precedence where they differ.

resources.title: Prompting best practices - Claude Platform Docs
resources.summary:
## Overview

This is Claude Platform documentation for prompt engineering with current Claude models, including guidance on clarity, examples, XML prompt structure, long-context inputs, output formatting, tool use, reasoning, agentic behavior, and migration from earlier model generations. It is intended for developers and application builders who want more reliable, controllable, and model-appropriate prompts, with model-specific pages recommended before applying the general techniques.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- Model-specific prompting guidance
  - Read the dedicated prompting page for the selected model first.
  - Account for differences in how individual Claude models respond.
  - Re-check model-specific findings against application-specific evaluations before transferring them to another model.
  - Models named in the reference include:
    - Claude Fable 5.1
    - Claude Mythos 5.1
    - Claude Fable 5
    - Claude Mythos 5
    - Claude Opus 5.5
    - Claude Opus 5
    - Claude Opus 4.8
    - Claude Opus 4.7
    - Claude Opus 4.6
    - Claude Sonnet 5.5
    - Claude Sonnet 5
    - Claude Sonnet 4.6
    - Claude Haiku 4.5

- Clear and direct prompting
  - State instructions explicitly.
  - Specify the desired output format and constraints.
  - Use numbered or bulleted steps when order or completeness matters.
  - Request unusually ambitious behavior explicitly instead of relying on inference.
  - Test prompt clarity using the “show it to a colleague” heuristic.

- Adding context and motivation
  - Explain why a requested behavior matters.
  - Provide context that helps Claude understand the application’s goals and norms.
  - Use explanations that allow Claude to generalize rather than memorizing one narrow case.

- Few-shot and multishot prompting
  - Use examples to steer output format, tone, and structure.
  - Make examples relevant to the actual use case.
  - Include diverse examples and edge cases.
  - Use 3–5 examples for the best results.
  - Wrap examples in `<example>` tags.
  - Group multiple examples in `<examples>` tags.
  - Ask Claude to evaluate examples for relevance and diversity.
  - Ask Claude to generate additional examples.

- XML prompt structuring
  - Use XML tags to separate instructions, context, examples, and variable inputs.
  - Use tags such as `<instructions>`, `<context>`, and `<input>`.
  - Prefer consistent, descriptive tag names.
  - Nest tags to represent natural document hierarchies.
  - Structure long documents and metadata with XML tags.

- Role prompting
  - Assign Claude a role in the system prompt to focus behavior and tone.
  - Use the Anthropic Python client example with:
    - `anthropic.Anthropic()`
    - `client.messages.create(...)`
    - `model`
    - `max_tokens`
    - `system`
    - `messages`
    - `message.content`

- Long-context prompting
  - Structure prompts containing large documents or data-rich inputs of 20k+ tokens.
  - Place long documents and inputs near the top of the prompt.
  - Put queries at the end.
  - Use XML tags for document content and metadata.
  - Ask Claude to quote relevant document passages before completing a task.
  - Reported effect: queries at the end improved response quality by up to 30% in tests, particularly for complex multidocument inputs.

- Model self-knowledge
  - Prompt Claude to identify itself correctly.
  - Prompt applications to use a particular API model string.
  - Example identity: Claude, created by Anthropic.
  - Example model string for Claude Opus 5.5: `claude-opus-5-5`.

- Communication style and verbosity
  - Account for the more concise, conversational, direct, and less verbose style of the latest models.
  - Recognize that Claude may skip summaries after tool calls.
  - Request a quick post-tool-use summary when progress visibility is important.
  - Claude Opus 5 has longer default user-facing responses.
  - For Claude Opus 5, prompt explicitly for conciseness because changing `effort` does not reliably control visible response length.
  - Claude Fable 5.1 may provide fewer user-facing updates during agentic work.
  - Request progress text explicitly and remove instructions that require such text to remain brief.

- Output-format control
  - Tell Claude what to do rather than only what not to do.
  - Use XML format indicators.
  - Match prompt formatting style to desired output style.
  - Provide detailed formatting instructions when markdown or structural control matters.
  - Minimize excessive markdown with an explicit prose-style instruction.
  - Reserve markdown for inline code, code blocks, and simple headings when appropriate.
  - Avoid unnecessary bold, italics, ordered lists, and unordered lists.
  - Use `<smoothly_flowing_prose_paragraphs>` tags when XML-style output control is useful.
  - Be careful with Claude Fable 5.1, which already uses less formatting and may lose necessary structure under an overly restrictive formatting block.

- LaTeX and mathematical formatting
  - Latest models default to LaTeX for mathematical expressions, equations, and technical explanations.
  - Request plain text when LaTeX is undesirable.
  - Prohibit LaTeX, MathJax, `\(`, `$`, and `\frac{}{}` when plain text is required.
  - Specify standard text-character alternatives such as `/`, `*`, and `^`.

- Document creation
  - Use explicit instructions for professional presentations.
  - Request thoughtful design elements.
  - Request visual hierarchy.
  - Request engaging animations where appropriate.
  - Latest models are described as strong at creating presentations, animations, and visual documents, often with usable first attempts.

- Migration from prefilled assistant responses
  - Claude 4.6 models and Claude Mythos Preview no longer support prefilled responses on the final assistant turn.
  - Requests containing prefilled assistant messages to these models return HTTP status `400`.
  - Earlier models continue to support prefills.
  - Assistant messages placed elsewhere in the conversation remain supported.
  - Migrate by replacing prefill-dependent behavior with explicit instructions.

- Tool-use triggering
  - Current models are trained for precise instruction following.
  - Explicitly direct the model to use tools or implement changes.
  - Define tools clearly.
  - Troubleshoot tool triggering.
  - Avoid vague requests such as “suggest changes” when implementation is intended.

- Proactive versus conservative action
  - Use a system prompt to make Claude implement changes by default.
  - Instruct Claude to infer useful likely actions when intent is unclear.
  - Instruct Claude to use tools to discover missing details rather than guessing.
  - Alternatively, use a system prompt to prevent unsolicited implementation or file changes.
  - For conservative behavior, require explicit requests before edits, modifications, or implementations.

- Tool-triggering calibration
  - Claude Opus 4.5 and Claude Opus 4.6 are more responsive to system prompts than previous models.
  - Prompts that previously reduced tool undertriggering may cause overtriggering on these models.
  - Replace aggressive language such as “CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...” with milder wording such as “Use this tool when...”.
  - Refer to the tool-use documentation for definitions and troubleshooting.

- Parallel tool calls
  - Current models run independent tool calls in parallel.
  - Parallel behavior can support:
    - Multiple speculative searches
    - Reading several files at once
    - Parallel bash commands
  - Increase the success rate of parallel tool calling to approximately 100% with explicit prompting.
  - Call independent tools simultaneously.
  - Keep dependent calls sequential.
  - Do not use placeholders or guess missing tool parameters.
  - Reduce parallel execution with an explicit sequential-execution instruction.
  - For Claude Fable 5.1 long agent loops, send the parallel-calls instruction as a turn-scoped system message after each round of tool results.

- Thinking and reasoning controls
  - Claude Opus 4.6 performs more upfront exploration than previous models, especially at higher `effort` settings.
  - Upfront exploration can improve final results but may also produce excessive context gathering or multiple research threads.
  - Replace blanket tool defaults with conditional instructions.
  - Remove over-prompting that may cause tool overtriggering.
  - Use a lower `effort` setting as a fallback if the model remains overly aggressive.
  - Excessive thinking can inflate thinking tokens and slow responses.
  - The extracted text ends while describing instructions that can constrain reasoning, so the complete recommendation is truncated.

- Reference structure
  - The page is organized into:
    1. Model-specific guidance
    2. Techniques for all current models
    3. Migration considerations
  - The general techniques section covers principles, output and formatting, tool use, thinking, and agentic systems.

## Detailed Notes

### Model selection and validation

The page positions model-specific guidance as the first step. Each listed model has its own prompting page, and the dedicated page should be read before the general techniques. The general guidance applies to current Claude models, including Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Mythos 5.1, Claude Fable 5, and Claude Mythos 5. When a technique was measured on a particular model, the documentation advises validating it with one’s own evaluations before applying it elsewhere.

### General prompting principles

Claude is described as responding well to clear, explicit instructions. The preferred approach is to make the desired output, constraints, and level of effort unambiguous. If the application wants “above and beyond” behavior, the prompt should request it explicitly.

The documentation’s golden rule is:

> Show your prompt to a colleague with minimal context on the task and ask them to follow it. If they would be confused, Claude will be too.

When sequence or completeness matters, instructions should be written as numbered or bulleted steps. Prompts should specify output format and constraints rather than assuming Claude will infer them.

Context and motivation can improve performance. Explaining why a behavior matters helps Claude understand the intended goal and generalize to related cases. The context should therefore provide the assumptions, workflow, or rationale that a human expert would need.

### Examples and XML structure

Examples are presented as one of the most reliable methods for controlling output format, tone, and structure. The page calls this few-shot or multishot prompting and recommends 3–5 examples.

Examples should be:

- **Relevant:** closely mirror the real use case.
- **Diverse:** cover edge cases and avoid causing Claude to infer unintended patterns.
- **Structured:** enclosed in `<example>` tags, with multiple examples grouped in `<examples>` tags.

Claude can also be asked to review an initial example set for relevance and diversity or to generate additional examples.

XML tags are recommended when prompts combine instructions, context, examples, and variable inputs. The suggested separation includes:

```xml
<instructions>
...
</instructions>

<context>
...
</context>

<input>
...
</input>
```

For hierarchical material, nested tags can represent structure:

```xml
<documents>
  <document index="1">
    ...
  </document>
</documents>
```

Tags should be descriptive and consistent across prompts.

### Role prompting and API example

A role in the system prompt focuses Claude’s behavior and tone. The documented Python example uses the Anthropic client:

```python
client = anthropic.Anthropic()

message = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-opus-5-5",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a helpful coding assistant specializing in Python.",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "How do I sort a list of dictionaries by key?"
        }
    ],
)

print(message.content)
```

The example sets `max_tokens=1024`, places the role instruction in `system`, and provides the user request as a message with `"role": "user"`.

### Long-context prompting

The page specifically addresses inputs of 20k+ tokens. The recommended ordering is:

1. Long documents and other longform data near the top.
2. The query, instructions, and examples after the long material.

Putting the query at the end is reported to improve response quality by up to 30% in tests, especially with complex, multidocument inputs.

When multiple documents are used, each can be wrapped in a `<document>` element, with separate subtags for content and source or other metadata:

```xml
<document>
  <document_content>
    ...
  </document_content>
  <source>
    ...
  </source>
</document>
```

For long-document tasks, the prompt can ask Claude to quote relevant passages first. This is intended to focus attention on relevant material and reduce interference from the rest of the document.

### Model identity prompts

The page provides two kinds of self-knowledge prompts.

For model identity:

> The assistant is Claude, created by Anthropic. The current model is Claude Opus 5.5.

For an LLM-powered application that needs a particular model string:

> When an LLM is needed, please default to Claude Opus 5.5 unless the user requests otherwise. The exact model string for Claude Opus 5.5 is `claude-opus-5-5`.

### Style and verbosity

Compared with previous models, current Claude models are described as:

- More direct and grounded, including in progress reports.
- More conversational, fluent, and colloquial.
- Less verbose, with summaries sometimes omitted for efficiency.

Because Claude may proceed directly to the next action after a tool call, applications that need visibility can request:

> After completing a task that involves tool use, provide a quick summary of the work you've done.

Claude Opus 5 is an exception: its default user-facing responses are longer, and changing `effort` does not reliably affect visible response length. The documented response is to request conciseness explicitly.

Claude Fable 5.1 has the opposite behavior during agentic work, producing fewer user-facing updates between tool calls. The prompt should explicitly request progress text, and any instruction that says the progress text must be brief should be removed.

### Output formatting

The page recommends positive formatting instructions. For example, rather than saying “Do not use markdown,” the prompt can say:

> Your response should be composed of smoothly flowing prose paragraphs.

XML indicators can be used when the output needs explicit structure:

> Write the prose sections of your response in `<smoothly_flowing_prose_paragraphs>` tags.

Prompt style can influence output style. If a desired output is not reliably produced, matching the prompt’s style to the desired output can help. For example, removing markdown from the prompt may reduce markdown in the response.

For stronger control over long-form output, the page provides a reusable instruction block:

```xml
<avoid_excessive_markdown_and_bullet_points>

When writing reports, documents, technical explanations, analyses, or any long-form content, write in clear, flowing prose using complete paragraphs and sentences. Use standard paragraph breaks for organization and reserve markdown primarily for `inline code`, code blocks (```...```), and simple headings (## and ###). Avoid using **bold** and *italics*.

DO NOT use ordered lists (1. ...) or unordered lists (*) unless:
a) you're presenting truly discrete items where a list format is the best option, or
b) the user explicitly requests a list or ranking

Instead of listing items with bullets or numbers, incorporate them naturally into sentences. This guidance applies especially to technical writing. Using prose instead of excessive formatting will improve user satisfaction. NEVER output a series of overly short bullet points.

Your goal is readable, flowing text that guides the reader naturally through ideas rather than fragmenting information into isolated points.

</avoid_excessive_markdown_and_bullet_points>
```

The page cautions that this block can suppress needed structure on Claude Fable 5.1 because that model already formats less than earlier models. In that case, the block should be removed or replaced with the shorter “Formatting in chat” rule referenced by the documentation.

### Mathematical notation

The current models default to LaTeX for mathematical expressions, equations, and technical explanations. To request plain text, the documentation suggests:

> Format your response in plain text only. Do not use LaTeX, MathJax, or any markup notation such as `\(`, `$`, or `\frac{}{}`. Write all math expressions using standard text characters (e.g., "/" for division, "*" for multiplication, and "^" for exponents).

### Document creation

For presentations and visual documents, the page provides this example:

> Create a professional presentation on [topic]. Include thoughtful design elements, visual hierarchy, and engaging animations where appropriate.

The stated expectation is that current models can usually produce usable document-creation output on the first attempt when given clear instructions.

### Prefill migration

Starting with Claude 4.6 models and Claude Mythos Preview, a final assistant-turn prefill is unsupported. A request containing such a prefill returns a `400` error.

The documented migration principle is to replace the prefill with explicit instructions. Earlier models continue to support prefills, and assistant messages in other conversation positions are not affected.

### Tool use and action control

Current models are more likely to provide suggestions rather than take action when the request is vague. The page recommends explicit tool-use direction and points to “Tool use with Claude” for tool definitions and trigger troubleshooting.

For proactive behavior, the documented system-prompt block is:

```xml
<default_to_action>
By default, implement changes rather than only suggesting them. If the user's intent is unclear, infer the most useful likely action and proceed, using tools to discover any missing details instead of guessing. Try to infer the user's intent about whether a tool call (e.g., file edit or read) is intended or not, and act accordingly.
</default_to_action>
```

For conservative behavior:

```xml
<do_not_act_before_instructions>
Do not jump into implementation or change files unless clearly instructed to make changes. When the user's intent is ambiguous, default to providing information, doing research, and providing recommendations rather than taking action. Only proceed with edits, modifications, or implementations when the user explicitly requests them.
</do_not_act_before_instructions>
```

Claude Opus 4.5 and Claude Opus 4.6 may be overly sensitive to aggressive system-prompt language. If earlier prompts were designed to prevent tool undertriggering, they may now cause overtriggering. The page recommends changing language such as:

> CRITICAL: You MUST use this tool when...

to a more moderate instruction such as:

> Use this tool when...

### Parallel tool calls

Current models run independent tool calls in parallel. The page says this can result in:

- Multiple speculative searches during research.
- Simultaneous reads of several files.
- Parallel bash commands, which can sometimes bottleneck system performance.

The following instruction is provided for maximum parallel efficiency:

```xml
<use_parallel_tool_calls>
If you intend to call multiple tools and there are no dependencies between the tool calls, make all of the independent tool calls in parallel. Prioritize calling tools simultaneously whenever the actions can be done in parallel rather than sequentially.

For example, when reading 3 files, run 3 tool calls in parallel to read all 3 files into context at the same time. Maximize use of parallel tool calls where possible to increase speed and efficiency.

However, if some tool calls depend on previous calls to inform dependent values like the parameters, do NOT call these tools in parallel and instead call them sequentially. Never use placeholders or guess missing parameters in tool calls.
</use_parallel_tool_calls>
```

The page says explicit parallel-calls prompting can raise the high success rate to approximately 100% and can also be used to adjust the aggressiveness of parallel behavior.

To reduce parallelism:

> Execute operations sequentially with brief pauses between each step to ensure stability.

For Claude Fable 5.1 in long agent loops, the parallel-call instruction should be sent as a turn-scoped system message after every round of tool results. This is linked to the page’s “Batch independent tool calls in agent loops” guidance.

### Thinking and reasoning

Claude Opus 4.6 performs more upfront exploration than previous models, particularly at higher `effort` settings. This can improve final answers, but it can also lead to extensive context gathering or multiple research threads.

The page recommends:

- Replacing blanket defaults with targeted conditions, such as “Use [tool] when it would enhance your understanding of the problem.”
- Removing over-prompting, such as “If in doubt, use [tool].”
- Lowering `effort` if the model remains overly aggressive.
- Adding explicit constraints if excessive reasoning inflates thinking tokens and slows responses.

The extracted page text is truncated during the discussion of reasoning constraints, so the complete wording and any additional recommended prompt pattern are not present in the supplied material.

## Key Concepts & References

- Prompt engineering for current Claude models.
- Model-specific prompting guidance and application-specific evaluation.
- Clear, explicit, sequential instructions.
- Context and motivation as prompt components.
- Few-shot prompting.
- Multishot prompting.
- Example diversity and edge-case coverage.
- XML-based prompt segmentation.
- Nested XML document structures.
- System-prompt role assignment.
- Anthropic Python client usage.
- `anthropic.Anthropic()`.
- `client.messages.create(...)`.
- Long-context prompt ordering.
- 20k+ token inputs.
- Quotation-first prompting for long documents.
- Model identity and model-string prompting.
- Output-style control.
- Positive instructions over negative instructions.
- Prose-style formatting.
- LaTeX, MathJax, and plain-text mathematical output.
- Document and presentation generation.
- Prefill deprecation and HTTP `400` errors.
- Explicit tool-use instructions.
- Proactive and conservative action policies.
- Tool overtriggering and undertriggering.
- Parallel tool execution.
- Dependent versus independent tool calls.
- Thinking-token control.
- `effort` settings.
- Claude Opus 4.6’s increased upfront exploration.
- Agent loops and turn-scoped system messages.
- Referenced related pages:
  - Prompting Claude Opus 5
  - Ask for user-facing progress updates
  - Formatting in chat
  - Tool use with Claude
  - Batch independent tool calls in agent loops

## Takeaways

- Read the model-specific prompting page before applying general techniques, and validate model-specific behavior with your own evaluations.
- Make instructions explicit, specify output constraints, and use ordered steps when sequence or completeness matters.
- Use 3–5 relevant, diverse, XML-wrapped examples to control Claude’s output format, tone, and structure.
- For long contexts, place long documents near the top and the query at the end; XML structure and quotation-first tasks can improve focus.
- Match prompting style to the desired response, and use explicit positive formatting instructions rather than relying on prohibitions.
- Control agent behavior explicitly: choose proactive implementation, conservative recommendation, maximum parallelism, or sequential execution as appropriate.
- Recent models may overtrigger tools, run independent tools in parallel, omit progress updates, or overexplore; tune prompts, `effort`, and system messages to the application’s needs.
- Prefills on the final assistant turn are unsupported for Claude 4.6 models and Claude Mythos Preview and produce HTTP `400` errors; migrate to explicit instructions.

resources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents | Anthropic
resources.summary:
## Overview

This Anthropic article presents context engineering as the evolution of prompt engineering for building reliable, steerable AI agents that operate across multiple inference turns and longer time horizons. It is aimed at engineers designing agent systems and explains how to curate the finite context supplied to an LLM through system prompts, tools, examples, retrieval, runtime exploration, and context-management techniques.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- Definition of **context** as the set of tokens included when sampling from an LLM.
- Definition of **context engineering** as optimizing the utility of context tokens under LLM constraints.
- Difference between **context engineering** and **prompt engineering**.
- The broader context state of an agent:
  - System instructions.
  - Tool definitions.
  - Model Context Protocol information.
  - External data.
  - Message history.
  - Retrieved information.
- The shift from one-shot prompting to agents operating across multiple inference turns.
- The iterative nature of context curation.
- Why context is a **finite resource**.
- **Context rot** and declining recall as context length increases.
- The LLM’s finite **attention budget**.
- Transformer architecture and the \(n^2\) pairwise relationships among \(n\) tokens.
- Architectural and training-distribution limitations for long-context processing.
- **Position encoding interpolation** for extending context length.
- Performance degradation in long-context retrieval and long-range reasoning.
- The goal of using the smallest set of high-signal tokens.
- System-prompt design:
  - Clear, direct language.
  - “Right altitude” for instructions.
  - Avoiding brittle hardcoded logic.
  - Avoiding vague, overly general guidance.
  - Balancing specificity and flexibility.
  - Organizing prompts into distinct sections.
  - XML tagging and Markdown headers.
  - Iterative prompt development based on failure modes.
- Tool design:
  - Efficient and token-conscious tool outputs.
  - Encouraging efficient agent behavior.
  - Self-contained tools.
  - Robustness to errors.
  - Clear intended use.
  - Minimal functional overlap.
  - Descriptive, unambiguous input parameters.
  - Avoiding bloated or ambiguous tool sets.
- Few-shot prompting:
  - Using examples to demonstrate expected behavior.
  - Preferring diverse, canonical examples.
  - Avoiding exhaustive edge-case prompts.
- Context retrieval and **agentic search**.
- Just-in-time context retrieval.
- Lightweight identifiers such as:
  - File paths.
  - Stored queries.
  - Web links.
- Runtime loading of data through tools.
- Claude Code’s database-analysis approach:
  - Writing targeted queries.
  - Storing results.
  - Using Bash commands such as `head` and `tail`.
  - Avoiding loading full data objects into context.
- Metadata as a behavioral signal:
  - File names.
  - Folder hierarchies.
  - Naming conventions.
  - Timestamps.
- Progressive disclosure.
- Incremental context discovery through exploration.
- Note-taking as a persistence strategy.
- Trade-offs of runtime exploration:
  - Slower execution.
  - Need for appropriate tools and navigation heuristics.
  - Risk of wasted context.
  - Risk of dead ends.
  - Risk of failing to identify key information.
- Hybrid retrieval strategies:
  - Pre-retrieving some information for speed.
  - Allowing autonomous exploration when appropriate.
- Claude Code as a hybrid agent:
  - `CLAUDE.md` files loaded up front.
  - `glob` and `grep` for runtime navigation.
  - Just-in-time file retrieval.
  - Avoiding stale indexing and complex syntax trees.
- Applicability of hybrid strategies to less dynamic domains such as legal or finance work.
- Long-horizon tasks:
  - Tasks lasting tens of minutes to hours.
  - Large codebase migrations.
  - Comprehensive research projects.
  - Work exceeding the context-window limit.
- Context pollution and information-relevance concerns for long-running agents.
- Techniques identified for long-horizon work:
  - Compaction.
  - Structured note-taking.
  - Multi-agent architectures.
- Compaction:
  - Summarizing a conversation near the context limit.
  - Reinitializing the context with the summary.
  - Preserving long-term coherence.
  - High-fidelity distillation.
  - Limiting performance degradation.
- Related Anthropic resources:
  - “Writing tools for AI agents – with AI agents”.
  - “Building effective AI agents”.
  - Anthropic prompt-engineering documentation.
- Tools and systems referenced:
  - Model Context Protocol.
  - Claude Code.
  - Bash.
  - `head`.
  - `tail`.
  - `glob`.
  - `grep`.
  - `CLAUDE.md`.

## Detailed Notes

### Context engineering versus prompt engineering

- The article defines **context** as:
  - “The set of tokens included when sampling from a large-language model (LLM).”
- The engineering problem is:
  - Optimizing the utility of those tokens.
  - Accounting for the inherent constraints of LLMs.
  - Consistently achieving a desired outcome.
- Anthropic characterizes context engineering as the natural progression of prompt engineering.
- **Prompt engineering** focuses primarily on writing and organizing instructions, especially system prompts, for effective outcomes.
- **Context engineering** is broader:
  - It curates and maintains the optimal set of tokens during inference.
  - It includes information that arrives outside the prompt.
  - It includes system instructions, tools, Model Context Protocol information, external data, message history, and other relevant context.
- The broader goal is sometimes expressed as determining:
  - “What configuration of context is most likely to generate our model’s desired behavior?”
- Anthropic recommends “thinking in context,” which means considering:
  - The holistic state available to the LLM at any given time.
  - The behaviors that state may produce.

### Why context management becomes necessary for agents

- Early applied AI systems often focused on prompts optimized for:
  - One-shot classification.
  - Text generation.
  - Everyday chat interactions.
- More capable agents operate across:
  - Multiple inference turns.
  - Longer time horizons.
  - Repeated tool use.
  - Continually changing information environments.
- An agent running in a loop produces more data that may be relevant to a later inference turn.
- That information must be continually refined rather than automatically accumulated.
- Context engineering is therefore iterative:
  - At each inference step, the engineer or agent selects what should enter the limited context window.
  - The possible information universe changes over time.

### Context rot and the attention budget

- The article uses **context rot** to describe the decline in a model’s ability to accurately recall information as the number of context tokens increases.
- Context rot has been observed through needle-in-a-haystack-style benchmarking.
- The degradation is not necessarily an abrupt failure:
  - Some models degrade more gently than others.
  - The article describes a “performance gradient rather than a hard cliff.”
- Models may remain highly capable at longer context lengths while showing reduced precision for:
  - Information retrieval.
  - Long-range reasoning.
- Context should therefore be treated as:
  - A finite resource.
  - A resource with diminishing marginal returns.
- Anthropic uses the analogy of human working memory to describe the LLM’s limited **attention budget**.
- Every token added to context consumes some of this budget.
- More context therefore increases the importance of careful token curation.

### Architectural basis for context degradation

- LLMs use the **transformer architecture**.
- In this architecture, every token can attend to every other token across the context.
- For \(n\) tokens, this produces:
  - \(n^2\) pairwise relationships.
- Increasing context length spreads the model’s ability to capture these relationships more thinly.
- This creates a tension between:
  - Larger context size.
  - Attention focus.
- Models also learn attention patterns from training-data distributions in which shorter sequences are more common than longer ones.
- As a result, models may have:
  - Less experience with long sequences.
  - Fewer specialized parameters for context-wide dependencies.
- **Position encoding interpolation** allows models to handle longer sequences by adapting them to the smaller context length used during original training.
- The article notes that this approach can involve degradation in token-position understanding.

### The guiding principle for effective context

- Because attention is constrained, good context engineering seeks:
  - The smallest possible set of high-signal tokens.
  - The set that maximizes the likelihood of the desired outcome.
- “Smallest” refers to removing low-value information, not necessarily minimizing the number of useful instructions.
- The article emphasizes that minimal context does not mean an inadequately short prompt:
  - The agent still needs enough information to adhere to the desired behavior.

### System prompts

- System prompts should be:
  - Extremely clear.
  - Written in simple, direct language.
  - Written at the “right altitude” for the agent.
- The article describes the right altitude as a **Goldilocks zone** between two failure modes:
  - Overly specific, brittle hardcoded logic.
  - Overly vague or general guidance.
- Hardcoded complex logic in prompts can:
  - Become fragile.
  - Increase maintenance complexity.
  - Restrict the model’s flexibility.
- Vague guidance can:
  - Fail to provide concrete signals about desired output.
  - Falsely assume that the model shares unstated context.
- Effective prompts should be:
  - Specific enough to guide behavior.
  - Flexible enough to provide useful heuristics.
- Anthropic recommends organizing system prompts into distinct sections, for example:
  - `<background_information>`
  - `<instructions>`
  - `## Tool guidance`
  - `## Output description`
- XML tags or Markdown headers can delineate these sections.
- The article suggests that exact prompt formatting may become less important as models become more capable.
- The system prompt should contain the minimal information that fully specifies expected behavior.
- The recommended development process is:
  1. Start with a minimal prompt.
  2. Test it using the best model available.
  3. Identify failures in the initial behavior.
  4. Add clear instructions and examples to address those failure modes.

### Tool design

- Tools let agents:
  - Operate in their environment.
  - Pull in additional context while working.
- Tools define the contract between:
  - The agent.
  - Its information and action space.
- Tool outputs should be token efficient.
- Tool design should also encourage efficient agent behavior.
- Anthropic recommends tools that are:
  - Well understood by LLMs.
  - Self-contained.
  - Robust to errors.
  - Extremely clear about intended use.
- Tools should have minimal overlap in functionality.
- Input parameters should be:
  - Descriptive.
  - Unambiguous.
  - Aligned with the model’s inherent strengths.
- A common failure mode is a bloated tool set that:
  - Covers too much functionality.
  - Creates ambiguity about which tool to use.
- Anthropic’s standard is that if a human engineer cannot definitively identify the appropriate tool, an AI agent should not be expected to do so reliably.
- A minimal viable tool set can support:
  - More reliable context maintenance.
  - More reliable context pruning over long interactions.

### Examples and few-shot prompting

- Anthropic continues to recommend examples, also known as few-shot prompting.
- However, teams should avoid stuffing prompts with a long list of edge cases.
- The preferred approach is to curate:
  - Diverse examples.
  - Canonical examples.
  - Examples that effectively portray expected behavior.
- The article emphasizes that examples communicate expected behavior more effectively than attempting to state every possible rule.
- Its phrasing is:
  - “For an LLM, examples are the ‘pictures’ worth a thousand words.”
- Across system prompts, tools, examples, and message history, Anthropic’s general guidance is:
  - Keep context informative.
  - Keep context tight.

### Runtime retrieval and agentic search

- Anthropic defines agents using a simple operational definition:
  - “LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop.”
- The article distinguishes this from the earlier distinction between LLM-based workflows and agents.
- As models become more capable, agent autonomy can increase:
  - More capable models can navigate nuanced problem spaces.
  - They can recover from errors more independently.
- Many AI-native applications use embedding-based retrieval before inference to surface relevant context.
- Agentic systems increasingly supplement pre-inference retrieval with **just-in-time context** strategies.
- Just-in-time systems do not preprocess all potentially relevant data in advance.
- Instead, they maintain lightweight references such as:
  - File paths.
  - Stored queries.
  - Web links.
- The agent uses tools at runtime to load the referenced data into context.
- The article uses Claude Code as an example of this approach for complex data analysis over large databases.
- In that example, the model can:
  - Write targeted queries.
  - Store results.
  - Run Bash commands such as `head` and `tail`.
  - Analyze large volumes of data.
  - Avoid loading full data objects into context.
- The approach is compared to human cognition:
  - Humans generally do not memorize entire corpora.
  - They use external organization and indexing systems such as file systems, inboxes, and bookmarks.
  - They retrieve information when needed.

### Metadata, exploration, and progressive disclosure

- References carry metadata that can guide behavior even when the referenced content is not loaded.
- File-system metadata can implicitly communicate purpose.
- For example, a file named `test_utils.py` inside a `tests` folder suggests a different role from the same filename inside `src/core_logic/`.
- Useful metadata includes:
  - File names.
  - Folder hierarchies.
  - Naming conventions.
  - Timestamps.
- These signals can help both humans and agents infer:
  - What information is likely to be useful.
  - When it may be relevant.
- Runtime retrieval enables **progressive disclosure**:
  - The agent incrementally discovers relevant context through exploration.
  - Each interaction supplies information that informs the next decision.
- Examples of signals discovered during exploration include:
  - File size as a proxy for complexity.
  - Naming conventions as clues to purpose.
  - Timestamps as proxies for relevance.
- Agents can build understanding layer by layer.
- They can maintain only necessary information in working memory and use note-taking for additional persistence.
- This self-managed context window helps the agent remain focused on relevant subsets rather than exhaustive, potentially irrelevant information.

### Limitations of runtime exploration

- Runtime exploration is slower than retrieving precomputed data.
- It requires deliberate engineering to provide:
  - The right tools.
  - Heuristics for navigating the information landscape.
- Without proper guidance, an agent may:
  - Misuse tools.
  - Chase dead ends.
  - Waste context.
  - Fail to identify key information.
- The appropriate level of autonomy depends on the task.
- A hybrid strategy may be effective:
  - Retrieve some data up front for speed.
  - Let the agent autonomously explore further when appropriate.
- Claude Code is described as using a hybrid model:
  - `CLAUDE.md` files are placed into context up front.
  - `glob` and `grep` enable runtime navigation.
  - Files are retrieved just in time.
  - This bypasses stale indexing and complex syntax trees.
- Hybrid strategies may be especially suitable for less dynamic domains such as legal or finance work.
- Anthropic expects agentic design to shift toward intelligent models navigating more independently, while retaining the practical recommendation:
  - “Do the simplest thing that works.”

### Long-horizon tasks

- Long-horizon tasks require agents to maintain:
  - Coherence.
  - Relevant context.
  - Goal-directed behavior.
- These tasks can involve sequences of actions whose token count exceeds the LLM’s context window.
- Examples given include:
  - Large codebase migrations.
  - Comprehensive research projects.
- These examples can run for:
  - Tens of minutes.
  - Multiple hours.
- Simply waiting for larger context windows does not remove the problem.
- The article argues that context windows of all sizes will continue to face:
  - Context pollution.
  - Information-relevance problems.
- These concerns are especially important when the strongest agent performance is desired.
- Anthropic identifies three specialized techniques for long-horizon work:
  - Compaction.
  - Structured note-taking.
  - Multi-agent architectures.

### Compaction

- **Compaction** is defined as:
  - Taking a conversation that is approaching the context-window limit.
  - Summarizing its contents.
  - Reinitializing a new context window with that summary.
- Compaction is presented as the first lever for context engineering when improving long-term coherence.
- Its purpose is to:
  - Distill the contents of a context window with high fidelity.
  - Preserve enough information for the agent to continue.
  - Minimize performance degradation.
- In the supplied page text, the article begins giving Claude Code as an example of compaction, but the example is truncated before its details are provided.

### Scope and truncation of the supplied page text

- The supplied text ends during the Claude Code compaction example.
- Structured note-taking and multi-agent architectures are named as long-horizon techniques, but their detailed mechanisms are not included in the provided excerpt.
- No installation instructions, API signatures, function definitions, or implementation code are present in the supplied text.
- The page text also does not provide the complete contents of the referenced Anthropic articles or documentation.

## Key Concepts & References

- **Context engineering** — Curating and maintaining the optimal information supplied during LLM inference.
- **Prompt engineering** — Writing and organizing instructions, especially system prompts, for effective model behavior.
- **Context** — The complete set of tokens available when sampling from an LLM.
- **Context rot** — Reduced information-recall accuracy as context length increases.
- **Attention budget** — The finite attention capacity that is consumed as more tokens are added.
- **Transformer architecture** — Architecture allowing tokens to attend to other tokens across the context, with \(n^2\) pairwise relationships for \(n\) tokens.
- **Position encoding interpolation** — A method for adapting models to longer sequences than those used in training.
- **System-prompt altitude** — Balancing specific behavioral constraints with flexible heuristics.
- **Tool design** — Creating self-contained, clear, robust, low-overlap tools with token-efficient outputs.
- **Few-shot prompting** — Using diverse, canonical examples to demonstrate expected behavior.
- **Agentic search** — Letting an agent use tools in a loop to retrieve and progressively discover information.
- **Just-in-time context** — Loading referenced information into context only when needed.
- **Embedding-based retrieval** — Pre-inference retrieval of relevant context using embeddings.
- **Progressive disclosure** — Incrementally revealing relevant context through exploration.
- **Hybrid retrieval** — Combining upfront retrieval with autonomous runtime exploration.
- **Compaction** — Summarizing a near-limit conversation and starting a new context window.
- Anthropic’s **Model Context Protocol (MCP)**.
- **Claude Code**.
- Bash commands including `head` and `tail`.
- `glob` and `grep`.
- `CLAUDE.md`.
- Anthropic references:
  - “Writing tools for AI agents – with AI agents”.
  - “Building effective AI agents”.
  - Anthropic prompt-engineering documentation.
- **Needle-in-a-haystack-style benchmarking**.
- **Long-horizon agents**.
- **Structured note-taking** and **multi-agent architectures**, named but not elaborated in the supplied excerpt.

## Takeaways

- Context engineering is broader than prompt engineering: it manages the entire token state supplied during inference, including tools, retrieved data, message history, and external information.
- Context is finite and has diminishing returns; every additional token consumes part of the model’s attention budget.
- The goal is not merely a short prompt, but the smallest set of high-signal information that fully supports the desired behavior.
- System prompts should be clear, appropriately specific, structured into sections, and developed iteratively from observed failure modes.
- Tool sets should be small, clear, robust, non-overlapping, and token-efficient.
- For long-running agents, Anthropic recommends curating context dynamically through just-in-time retrieval, progressive disclosure, metadata, and—when appropriate—hybrid upfront and runtime retrieval.
- For work that exceeds the context window, compaction is described as a primary mechanism for preserving long-term coherence while limiting performance degradation.
