resources.title: [2305.14314] QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
resources.summary:
## Overview

This arXiv resource is the abstract and metadata page for **“QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs,”** submitted on 23 May 2023 by Tim Dettmers, Artidoro Pagnoni, Ari Holtzman, and Luke Zettlemoyer. It is intended for researchers and practitioners interested in memory-efficient adaptation of large language models and provides a concise overview of QLoRA, its major memory-saving components, the Guanaco model family, experimental scope, evaluation findings, and released artifacts; the linked full paper, experimental HTML, and TeX source contain the detailed technical treatment.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- **Memory-efficient finetuning of large language models**
  - Reducing memory enough to finetune a **65B-parameter model on one 48 GB GPU**.
  - Preserving the task performance of full **16-bit finetuning**.
  - Enabling model scales that are infeasible with regular finetuning, including **33B- and 65B-parameter models**.

- **QLoRA training architecture**
  - Keeping the pretrained language model **frozen**.
  - Quantizing the pretrained model to **4 bits**.
  - Backpropagating gradients through the frozen quantized model into **Low Rank Adapters (LoRA)**.
  - Adapting quantized language models without storing full-precision trainable copies of the base model.

- **4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)**
  - A new **4-bit data type**.
  - Designed to be **information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights**.
  - Used as one of QLoRA’s principal memory-saving innovations.

- **Double quantization**
  - Quantizing the **quantization constants**.
  - Reducing the average memory footprint associated with quantized model storage.

- **Paged optimizers**
  - Memory management for temporary increases in memory use.
  - Handling **memory spikes** during finetuning.

- **Guanaco model family**
  - The paper’s best-performing model family.
  - Developed using QLoRA.
  - Evaluated on the **Vicuna benchmark**.
  - Reported as outperforming all previous openly released models on that benchmark.
  - Reported as reaching **99.3% of ChatGPT’s performance level**.
  - Reported to require only **24 hours of finetuning on a single GPU** for the stated result.

- **Experimental scale and model diversity**
  - More than **1,000 finetuned models**.
  - Evaluation across **8 instruction datasets**.
  - Analysis of instruction-following and chatbot performance.
  - Coverage of multiple model families:
    - **LLaMA**
    - **T5**
  - Coverage of model scales that regular finetuning would make infeasible.

- **Instruction tuning and dataset quality**
  - Finetuning on a **small, high-quality dataset**.
  - Connection between dataset quality and state-of-the-art results.
  - Use of smaller models to exceed prior state-of-the-art systems.

- **Chatbot evaluation**
  - Evaluation based on both:
    - **Human evaluation**
    - **GPT-4 evaluation**
  - Finding that GPT-4 evaluations are a **cheap and reasonable alternative to human evaluation**.
  - Analysis of chatbot performance on instruction-following tasks.

- **Chatbot benchmark reliability**
  - Examination of the ability of current chatbot benchmarks to measure chatbot performance accurately.
  - Reported conclusion that such benchmarks are **not trustworthy enough to accurately evaluate chatbot performance levels**.

- **Failure analysis**
  - Analysis of selected cases in which **Guanaco underperforms ChatGPT**.
  - Examination of the kinds of prompts or interactions that expose remaining performance gaps.

- **Open release**
  - Release of the paper’s models and code.
  - Release of **CUDA kernels for 4-bit training**.
  - Availability through the arXiv page’s PDF, experimental HTML, and TeX-source links.

- **Publication and citation metadata**
  - arXiv identifier: **arXiv:2305.14314**.
  - Version: **arXiv:2305.14314v1**.
  - Subject category: **Machine Learning (cs.LG)**.
  - DOI: **https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2305.14314**.
  - Listed as an **Extended NeurIPS submission**.

## Detailed Notes

**Resource scope.** The supplied page is the arXiv abstract and bibliographic landing page rather than the paper’s complete body. It gives the central claims and experimental conclusions but does not include implementation code, mathematical derivations, complete training hyperparameters, dataset names, benchmark prompts, or procedural setup instructions. Those details would need to be obtained from the linked PDF, experimental HTML, or TeX source.

**Core finetuning mechanism.** QLoRA is presented as an efficient finetuning method for pretrained language models. Its base model is kept **frozen** and represented using **4-bit quantization**, while gradients are backpropagated through that quantized model into **LoRA adapters**. The page does not provide LoRA’s rank, target-module configuration, initialization procedure, learning rate, optimizer settings, or adapter parameter count.

**Memory objective.** The headline system-level claim is that QLoRA reduces memory sufficiently to finetune a **65B-parameter language model on a single 48 GB GPU**. The abstract frames this as retaining the task performance associated with full **16-bit finetuning**. It does not give a complete memory breakdown on this page.

**4-bit NormalFloat.** QLoRA introduces **4-bit NormalFloat**, abbreviated **NF4**, as a new data type. The specific claim made on the page is that NF4 is **information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights**. No formal information-theoretic derivation, codebook construction procedure, or numerical comparison with other 4-bit formats appears in the supplied text.

**Double quantization.** The second quantization-level innovation is **double quantization**. The page explains that the memory-saving idea is to quantize the **quantization constants**, thereby reducing their average memory cost. The page does not state the bit width used for the constants, the exact block size, or the resulting numerical compression factor.

**Paged optimizers.** The third named memory-management component is **paged optimizers**. These are introduced as a way to manage **memory spikes** during training. The abstract does not expose the paging API, page-management policy, optimizer state representation, or comparison against standard optimizer implementations.

**Guanaco results.** The paper calls its strongest model family **Guanaco**. On the **Vicuna benchmark**, the abstract reports that Guanaco outperforms all previously openly released models and reaches **99.3% of the performance level of ChatGPT**. The reported training requirement for this result is **24 hours of finetuning on a single GPU**. The page does not identify the exact Guanaco model size, quantization configuration, hardware model, inference settings, or evaluation protocol for this result.

**Experimental coverage.** The authors report using QLoRA to finetune **more than 1,000 models**. Their analysis spans:
- **8 instruction datasets**
- Instruction-following performance
- Chatbot performance
- **LLaMA** model types
- **T5** model types
- **33B- and 65B-parameter** scales

The emphasis is not only on reducing memory but also on showing that QLoRA can support experiments at scales considered infeasible under regular finetuning.

**Dataset-quality result.** The abstract reports that finetuning on a **small, high-quality dataset** can produce state-of-the-art results even when using smaller models than the previous state of the art. The supplied page does not identify the dataset or enumerate the model sizes used for this specific result.

**Human and GPT-4 evaluation.** The paper provides chatbot-performance analysis based on both **human evaluation** and **GPT-4 evaluation**. Its reported conclusion is that GPT-4 evaluation is a **cheap and reasonable alternative to human evaluation**. The page does not provide agreement statistics, prompting details, judge configuration, sample counts, cost measurements, or the exact scoring rubric.

**Benchmark reliability.** The authors also find that current chatbot benchmarks are not reliable indicators of chatbot performance levels. This is an important negative result: high benchmark standing may not by itself establish that a chatbot performs accurately across relevant use cases. The supplied text does not identify which specific benchmarks are included in this reliability analysis beyond the explicit mention of Vicuna.

**Failure analysis.** The paper includes a “lemon-picked” analysis of cases where **Guanaco fails compared with ChatGPT**. The page indicates that the purpose is to identify where Guanaco falls short, but it does not include examples, categories of failure, or quantitative error rates.

**Artifacts and availability.** The authors state that they release:
- The paper’s models
- The associated code
- **CUDA kernels for 4-bit training**

The arXiv page provides links to the PDF, experimental HTML, and TeX source. The page also exposes related-code and model-platform links through arXiv’s integration features, but it does not provide repository names or installation commands.

**Bibliographic details.**
- **Title:** *QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs*
- **Authors:** Tim Dettmers, Artidoro Pagnoni, Ari Holtzman, Luke Zettlemoyer
- **Submitted:** 23 May 2023
- **arXiv submission timestamp:** Tue, 23 May 2023 17:50:33 UTC
- **Category:** Machine Learning (`cs.LG`)
- **Comment:** Extended NeurIPS submission
- **File size shown on page:** 568 KB

**Limitations of the supplied page.** It does not include:
- A formal definition of QLoRA’s update rule.
- LoRA rank or adapter placement details.
- The exact NF4 encoding or information-theoretic proof.
- Exact double-quantization settings.
- Paged-optimizer implementation details.
- Training hyperparameters.
- Dataset names or examples.
- Complete benchmark tables.
- Hardware specifications beyond the stated 48 GB GPU and single-GPU training setting.
- Installation or reproduction steps.
- Detailed limitations of the method.

## Key Concepts & References

- **QLoRA** — finetuning method that sends gradients through a frozen 4-bit quantized model into LoRA adapters.
- **Low Rank Adapters (LoRA)** — trainable low-rank adaptation mechanism used as QLoRA’s update path.
- **4-bit NormalFloat (NF4)** — information-theoretically optimal 4-bit data type for normally distributed weights.
- **Double quantization** — quantization of quantization constants to lower average memory use.
- **Paged optimizers** — memory-spike management for finetuning.
- **Guanaco** — model family produced with QLoRA and evaluated on the Vicuna benchmark.
- **Vicuna benchmark** — benchmark used for the reported Guanaco comparison with prior open models and ChatGPT.
- **ChatGPT** — comparison system whose reported performance level Guanaco approaches.
- **Instruction tuning** — finetuning regime analyzed across eight instruction datasets.
- **LLaMA** and **T5** — model families included in the experimental analysis.
- **GPT-4-based evaluation** — judge-based alternative to human chatbot evaluation.
- **Human evaluation** — evaluation modality used to assess chatbot performance.
- **CUDA kernels for 4-bit training** — released low-level training components.
- **arXiv:2305.14314** — identifier for the QLoRA paper.

## Takeaways

- QLoRA finetunes large language models by keeping the base model **frozen and quantized to 4 bits** while training **LoRA adapters**.
- The paper reports that a **65B-parameter model can be finetuned on one 48 GB GPU** while preserving the task performance of full 16-bit finetuning.
- Its three named memory-saving innovations are **NF4**, **double quantization**, and **paged optimizers**.
- The **Guanaco** family reaches a reported **99.3% of ChatGPT’s performance level on Vicuna**, following **24 hours of single-GPU finetuning**.
- The study covers more than **1,000 models**, eight instruction datasets, LLaMA and T5 architectures, and scales such as 33B and 65B.
- A small, high-quality instruction dataset can be sufficient for state-of-the-art results.
- GPT-4 evaluation is reported as a cheap, reasonable alternative to human evaluation, while current chatbot benchmarks are characterized as unreliable.
- The authors release models, code, and **CUDA kernels for 4-bit training**.

resources.title: PEFT · Hugging Face
resources.summary:
## Overview

Hugging Face PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning) is a library for adapting large pretrained models to downstream applications without updating all model parameters. It is intended for users who want to reduce the computational and storage requirements of training, storing, and deploying large language and other large models, while obtaining performance described as comparable to full fine-tuning.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)
  - Adapting large pretrained models to downstream tasks.
  - Avoiding full-model fine-tuning.
  - Reducing training-time computational costs.
  - Reducing model storage costs.
  - Making large-model adaptation more accessible on consumer hardware.
  - Maintaining performance comparable to fully fine-tuned models.
- PEFT as an adaptation framework
  - Arbitrary approaches to adapting existing models.
  - Modifying model weights.
  - Wrapping model layers.
  - Manipulating key-value caches (KV-caches).
  - Acting as a reference implementation for fine-tuning methods.
- Integration with Hugging Face libraries
  - Transformers integration.
  - Diffusers integration.
  - Accelerate integration.
  - Faster loading of large models.
  - Faster training of large models.
  - Easier use of large models for inference.
- Large-model use cases
  - Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs).
  - Adapting other large pretrained models.
  - Storing adapted models with fewer parameter updates.
  - Running model-adaptation workflows on consumer hardware.
- Project resources
  - Link or prompt to update or contribute through the project’s GitHub repository.

## Detailed Notes

### Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning

PEFT stands for **Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning**. It provides a way to adapt an existing large pretrained model to a downstream application without fine-tuning every parameter in that model.

The motivation is cost: updating all parameters of a large model is described as prohibitively expensive. PEFT instead fine-tunes only a small number of additional model parameters, which significantly lowers computational and storage costs.

The library presents this reduction in cost as compatible with performance comparable to a fully fine-tuned model. Its practical effect is to make it more feasible to:

- Train large language models.
- Store large models and their task-specific adaptations.
- Adapt other large models.
- Perform these operations on consumer hardware.

### Model Adaptation as a General Framework

PEFT is not characterized only as a collection of individual adaptation techniques. It can also be viewed as a framework for arbitrary methods of model adaptation.

Examples of adaptation mechanisms given on the page include:

- **Modifying weights**
- **Wrapping layers**
- **Manipulating key-value caches (KV-caches)**

This framing means developers can use PEFT as a general abstraction for model-adaptation methods while the library also serves as a reference implementation for many fine-tuning approaches.

The page does not name particular PEFT algorithms, methods, parameter schemes, layer types, configuration classes, or API functions.

### Hugging Face Library Integrations

PEFT is integrated with three named Hugging Face libraries:

- **Transformers**
- **Diffusers**
- **Accelerate**

These integrations provide a faster and easier workflow for:

- Loading large models.
- Training large models.
- Using large models for inference.

No installation commands, code examples, package names, versions, API signatures, or configuration defaults appear in the supplied page text.

### Project Development

The page includes an **“Update on GitHub”** prompt, indicating that project development and updates are associated with a GitHub repository. The supplied text does not include the repository URL, contribution instructions, release details, or version information.

## Key Concepts & References

- **PEFT (Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning):** Fine-tuning a small number of additional parameters rather than all model parameters.
- **Pretrained model adaptation:** Reusing a large pretrained model for a downstream application.
- **Computational efficiency:** Reducing the computation required for model adaptation.
- **Storage efficiency:** Reducing the storage cost associated with training and storing large-model adaptations.
- **Consumer hardware:** Making large-model training and adaptation more accessible.
- **Model-weight modification:** One form of model adaptation supported by the broader PEFT framework.
- **Layer wrapping:** Another adaptation mechanism described by the resource.
- **KV-cache manipulation:** Adaptation through changes to key-value caches.
- **Transformers:** Hugging Face library integrated with PEFT.
- **Diffusers:** Hugging Face library integrated with PEFT.
- **Accelerate:** Hugging Face library integrated with PEFT.
- **GitHub:** Platform referenced for project updates.

## Takeaways

- PEFT adapts large pretrained models by updating only a small number of additional parameters instead of all parameters.
- The goal is to significantly reduce computational and storage costs relative to full fine-tuning.
- PEFT is presented as making large-model training and storage more accessible on consumer hardware.
- It can serve both as a general adaptation framework and as a reference implementation for fine-tuning methods.
- Supported adaptation ideas described on the page include modifying weights, wrapping layers, and manipulating KV-caches.
- PEFT integrates with Transformers, Diffusers, and Accelerate for loading, training, and inference workflows.

resources.title: Bitsandbytes · Hugging Face
resources.summary:
## Overview

The Hugging Face Bitsandbytes documentation describes a lightweight Python library for reducing the memory requirements of large language models through hardware-accelerated quantization and optimized numerical operations. It is intended for users loading, distributing, and training large models with Hugging Face Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT, and compatible hardware, with practical guidance for 8-bit LLM.int8() and 4-bit QLoRA workflows.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- Bitsandbytes as a lightweight Python wrapper around hardware-accelerator functions
- Reducing LLM memory footprint with quantization
- Quantized linear layers:
  - `Linear8bitLt`
  - `Linear4bit`
  - Replacement of standard `torch.nn.Linear` layers
- Optimized 8-bit optimizers through the `bitsandbytes.optim` module
- Matrix multiplication using quantized formats
- 8-bit LLM.int8() quantization
  - Dynamic preservation of higher precision for critical computations
  - Reduction of information loss in sensitive model components
- 4-bit QLoRA quantization
  - Greater model compression
  - Preservation of trainability
  - Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) trainable weights
- Installation with Transformers and Accelerate
  - `pip install --upgrade transformers accelerate bitsandbytes`
  - Compilation from source through the bitsandbytes installation guide
- Supported hardware:
  - NVIDIA GPUs with CUDA 11.8–13.0
  - Intel XPU
  - Intel Gaudi HPU
  - CPU
  - Supported operating systems and CPU architectures
- Hardware requirements for:
  - 8-bit optimizers
  - `LLM.int8()`
  - NF4/FP4 quantization
- `BitsAndBytesConfig`
- Loading quantized models with:
  - `AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained()`
  - `load_in_8bit=True`
  - `load_in_4bit=True`
  - `device_map="auto"`
- Accelerate compatibility and `torch.nn.Linear` eligibility
- 8-bit memory reduction and multi-GPU distribution
- Non-linear module precision:
  - Default behavior for modules such as `torch.nn.LayerNorm`
  - Changing precision with `dtype`
  - Loading configured precision with `dtype="auto"`
  - Reading precision from `config.json`
- Querying dtype through:
  - `model.model.decoder.layers[-1].final_layer_norm.weight.dtype`
- Publishing quantized models to the Hugging Face Hub:
  - Version requirements
  - `push_to_hub()`
  - Upload order for `quantization_config.json` and quantized weights
- Inspecting memory use with:
  - `get_memory_footprint()`
- Reloading quantized models without passing `quantization_config`
- Limitation of 8-bit and 4-bit training:
  - Only extra parameters are supported
- CPU–GPU offloading for 8-bit models:
  - `llm_int8_enable_fp32_cpu_offload=True`
  - CPU weights stored in `float32`
  - Custom `device_map`
- LLM.int8() outlier thresholds:
  - Definition of an outlier
  - `llm_int8_threshold`
  - Default threshold of 6
  - Threshold sensitivity for unstable models
  - Threshold-performance and accuracy trade-off
- Skipping module conversion:
  - `llm_int8_skip_modules`
  - Full-precision BLOOM `lm_head`
  - Avoiding quantization instability
- 8-bit fine-tuning through PEFT
  - Supported examples such as `flan-t5-large` and `facebook/opt-6.7b`
  - Automatic GPU loading for training
  - Custom device maps
  - Restriction of `device_map="auto"` to inference
- 4-bit compute precision:
  - Default `float32`
  - `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16`
  - Computation speedup
- Normal Float 4:
  - NF4 definition
  - Origin in the QLoRA paper
  - Suitability for normally distributed weight initialization
  - `bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4"`
  - Inference performance and dtype consistency
- Nested quantization:
  - `bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True`
  - Second quantization of already quantized weights
  - Additional saving of 0.4 bits per parameter
  - Llama-13b fine-tuning example on a 16GB NVIDIA T4
- Dequantization:
  - `dequantize()`
  - Restoration to original precision
  - Potential quality loss
  - GPU-memory requirement
- User-friendly quantization through the bitsandbytes community space
- Links to additional resources:
  - “A Gentle Introduction to 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for transformers at scale using Hugging Face Transformers, Accelerate and bitsandbytes”
  - “Making LLMs even more accessible with bitsandbytes, 4-bit quantization and QLoRA”
  - 4-bit quantization notebook
  - GitHub repository and source installation guide

## Detailed Notes

### 1. Library purpose and core components

Bitsandbytes provides quantization tools for LLMs through a lightweight Python wrapper around hardware-accelerator functions. Its primary purpose is to make large models usable with limited computational resources by reducing their memory footprint.

The library provides three core capability groups:

- **Quantized linear layers**
  - `Linear8bitLt` and `Linear4bit` replace standard PyTorch linear layers with memory-efficient quantized alternatives.
- **Optimized optimizers**
  - The `bitsandbytes.optim` module provides 8-bit versions of common optimizers, allowing large-model training with lower memory requirements.
- **Matrix multiplication**
  - Optimized matrix multiplication operations can operate using quantized formats.

A user-friendly quantization interface is also available through the bitsandbytes community space.

### 2. Installation

Install bitsandbytes together with current versions of Transformers and Accelerate:

```bash
pip install --upgrade transformers accelerate bitsandbytes
```

For a source build, the documentation directs users to the bitsandbytes installation guide. The page also points to the bitsandbytes repository for platform feedback and testing information.

### 3. Hardware compatibility

Bitsandbytes supports:

- NVIDIA GPUs running CUDA versions 11.8–13.0
- Intel XPU
- Intel Gaudi HPU
- CPU

Additional platform support is described as an ongoing effort.

#### NVIDIA GPUs and CUDA

The NVIDIA backend supports:

- Linux x86-64
- Linux aarch64
- Windows

Feature requirements listed in the documentation are:

| Feature | Minimum hardware requirement |
|---|---|
| 8-bit optimizers | NVIDIA Pascal, such as GTX 10X0 series or P100, or newer |
| `LLM.int8()` | NVIDIA Turing, such as RTX 20X0 series or T4, or newer |
| NF4/FP4 quantization | NVIDIA Pascal, such as GTX 10X0 series or P100, or newer |

The optimizer and NF4/FP4 rows are marked with an asterisk in the source, but no further meaning for that marker is provided in the extracted text.

#### Intel XPU

Supported on:

- Linux x86-64
- Windows x86-64

#### Intel Gaudi HPU

Supported on Linux x86-64 for:

- Gaudi2
- Gaudi3

#### CPU

Supported on:

- Linux x86-64
- Linux aarch64
- Windows x86-64

### 4. Basic 8-bit model loading

A model is quantized by passing a `BitsAndBytesConfig` to `from_pretrained()`. According to the page, this approach works with models in any modality provided that the model:

- Supports Accelerate
- Contains `torch.nn.Linear` layers

The basic configuration is:

```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_8bit=True)

model_8bit = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "bigscience/bloom-1b7",
    device_map="auto",
    quantization_config=quantization_config
)
```

Key behavior:

- 8-bit quantization halves model memory usage.
- For large models, `device_map="auto"` distributes weights efficiently across all available GPUs.

### 5. Precision of non-quantized modules

By default, modules other than quantized linear layers, such as `torch.nn.LayerNorm`, use PyTorch’s default dtype. Their dtype can be changed through the `dtype` argument.

Using:

```python
dtype="auto"
```

loads those modules in the dtype declared in the model’s `config.json`.

Example:

```python
import torch

from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_8bit=True)

model_8bit = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "facebook/opt-350m",
    device_map="auto",
    quantization_config=quantization_config,
    dtype="auto"
)

model_8bit.model.decoder.layers[-1].final_layer_norm.weight.dtype
```

The final expression checks the resulting `LayerNorm` weight dtype.

### 6. Pushing and reloading quantized models

A quantized 8-bit model cannot be pushed to the Hub unless the latest versions of both Transformers and bitsandbytes are installed.

With current versions, call:

```python
model.push_to_hub("bloom-560m-8bit")
```

The upload order is:

1. `quantization_config.json`
2. Quantized model weights

Example:

```python
from transformers import (
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    AutoTokenizer,
    BitsAndBytesConfig,
)

quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_8bit=True)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "bigscience/bloom-560m",
    device_map="auto",
    quantization_config=quantization_config
)

model.push_to_hub("bloom-560m-8bit")
```

A quantized model stored this way is reloaded with `from_pretrained()` **without** supplying `quantization_config` again:

```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "{your_username}/bloom-560m-8bit",
    device_map="auto"
)
```

The page also notes:

- 8-bit and 4-bit training support only **extra parameters**.
- Current memory consumption can be checked with:

```python
print(model.get_memory_footprint())
```

### 7. LLM.int8() CPU offloading

An 8-bit model can offload weights between CPU and GPU so that a model too large for GPU memory can still be loaded.

Configuration:

```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    llm_int8_enable_fp32_cpu_offload=True
)
```

Important precision detail:

- Weights dispatched to the CPU are stored as `float32`.
- Those CPU-offloaded weights are not converted to 8-bit.

A custom device map can place all model components on GPU 0 except `lm_head`, which is sent to the CPU:

```python
device_map = {
    "transformer.word_embeddings": 0,
    "transformer.word_embeddings_layernorm": 0,
    "lm_head": "cpu",
    "transformer.h": 0,
    "transformer.ln_f": 0,
}
```

The model is loaded with both the map and configuration:

```python
model_8bit = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "bigscience/bloom-1b7",
    dtype="auto",
    device_map=device_map,
    quantization_config=quantization_config,
)
```

### 8. LLM.int8() outlier thresholds

An **outlier** is defined as a hidden-state value greater than a specified threshold. Outlier values are computed in `fp16`.

The page explains that hidden-state values are often distributed approximately within:

\[
[-3.5, 3.5]
\]

but large models can have much wider distributions, including:

\[
[-60, 6]
\quad \text{or} \quad
[6, 60]
\]

Quantization performs well for values around magnitude 5, but performance deteriorates significantly beyond that range. The recommended default outlier threshold is:

\[
6
\]

A lower threshold may be useful for less stable cases, including:

- Small models
- Fine-tuning

The threshold is controlled with `llm_int8_threshold`. For example:

```python
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, BitsAndBytesConfig

model_id = "bigscience/bloom-1b7"

quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    llm_int8_threshold=0.0,
    llm_int8_enable_fp32_cpu_offload=True
)

model_8bit = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    dtype="auto",
    device_map=device_map,
    quantization_config=quantization_config,
)
```

Setting the threshold to `0.0` can significantly accelerate inference, but may reduce accuracy.

### 9. Skipping 8-bit module conversion

Converting every module to 8-bit can introduce instability. Some modules are more stable when left in full precision. Such modules can be named in `llm_int8_skip_modules`.

For BLOOM, the example skips `lm_head` because it shares weights with the input embeddings:

```python
from transformers import (
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    AutoTokenizer,
    BitsAndBytesConfig,
)

model_id = "bigscience/bloom-1b7"

quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    llm_int8_skip_modules=[
        "lm_head"
    ],
)

model_8bit = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    dtype="auto",
    device_map="auto",
    quantization_config=quantization_config,
)
```

### 10. Fine-tuning with 8-bit quantization

The PEFT library can fine-tune large models such as:

- `flan-t5-large`
- `facebook/opt-6.7b`

with 8-bit quantization.

Training behavior and restrictions:

- `device_map` need not be supplied because PEFT automatically loads the model onto a GPU.
- A custom device map can still be provided.
- `device_map="auto"` should be used only for inference.

The page’s general limitation remains important: 8-bit and 4-bit training applies to training **extra parameters**, rather than the full quantized model.

### 11. QLoRA and 4-bit loading

QLoRA is the page’s 4-bit quantization technique. It compresses models further while preserving trainability by adding a small number of trainable low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, weights.

The page’s 4-bit examples use:

```python
BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True)
```

The example model is then loaded through `AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained()`.

### 12. 4-bit compute data type

The 4-bit compute dtype defaults to `float32`. It can be changed to `bf16` through `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype` to speed up computation:

```python
import torch

from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig

quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16
)
```

The relevant configuration fields are:

| Argument | Meaning in the page |
|---|---|
| `load_in_4bit=True` | Loads the model in 4-bit mode |
| `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype` | Controls the computation dtype; default is `float32` |
| `dtype` | Controls model loading dtype, with `"auto"` using the model configuration |

### 13. Normal Float 4 and quantization type

Normal Float 4, or **NF4**, is a 4-bit data type introduced in the QLoRA paper. It is adapted for weights whose initialization follows a normal distribution.

Recommended training configuration:

```python
from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig

nf4_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
)

model_nf4 = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    dtype="auto",
    quantization_config=nf4_config
)
```

Guidance:

- Use NF4 when training a 4-bit base model.
- During inference, `bnb_4bit_quant_type` does not have a large performance impact.
- For consistency with the stored model weights, use matching `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype` and `dtype` values.

### 14. Nested quantization

Nested or double quantization applies a second quantization to weights that are already quantized. The page states that it:

- Saves additional memory
- Has no additional performance cost
- Saves an additional `0.4` bits per parameter

Configuration:

```python
from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig

double_quant_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
)

model_double_quant = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "meta-llama/Llama-2-13b-chat-hf",
    dtype="auto",
    quantization_config=double_quant_config
)
```

The documented use case is fine-tuning a Llama-13b model on:

- A 16GB NVIDIA T4 GPU
- Sequence length 1024
- Batch size 1
- Gradient accumulation enabled for 4 steps

### 15. Dequantization

A quantized model can be converted back to its original precision with `model.dequantize()`:

```python
from transformers import (
    AutoModelForCausalLM,
    BitsAndBytesConfig,
    AutoTokenizer,
)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "facebook/opt-125m",
    BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True)
)

model.dequantize()
```

Cautions:

- Dequantization may cause some quality loss.
- GPU memory must be sufficient to hold the dequantized model.

## Key Concepts & References

- **bitsandbytes**: Lightweight Python wrapper providing hardware-accelerated quantization and numerical operations.
- **`Linear8bitLt`**: Memory-efficient 8-bit replacement for a standard PyTorch linear layer.
- **`Linear4bit`**: Memory-efficient 4-bit replacement for a standard PyTorch linear layer.
- **`bitsandbytes.optim`**: Module containing 8-bit versions of common optimizers.
- **`LLM.int8()`**: 8-bit quantization method that dynamically retains higher precision for important computations.
- **QLoRA**: 4-bit quantization method that preserves trainability through a small set of LoRA weights.
- **LoRA**: Low-rank adaptation weights inserted by QLoRA for trainability.
- **NF4**: Normal Float 4, a QLoRA-derived 4-bit type for normally distributed weight initialization.
- **Nested quantization**: A second quantization pass that saves an additional 0.4 bits per parameter.
- **`BitsAndBytesConfig`**: Main Transformers configuration object for bitsandbytes quantization.
- **Accelerate**: Required support for the model-loading workflow described on the page.
- **PEFT**: Library used for fine-tuning models under 8-bit quantization.
- **Hugging Face Hub**: Supports publishing and reloading quantized models under the stated version requirements.
- **“A Gentle Introduction to 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for transformers at scale using Hugging Face Transformers, Accelerate and bitsandbytes”**: Additional 8-bit quantization resource.
- **“Making LLMs even more accessible with bitsandbytes, 4-bit quantization and QLoRA”**: Additional 4-bit and QLoRA resource.
- **bitsandbytes GitHub repository**: Installation, platform feedback, and testing information.
- **bitsandbytes community space**: User-friendly quantization option.

## Takeaways

- Bitsandbytes reduces LLM memory use through 8-bit and 4-bit quantization, optimized linear layers and matrix multiplication, and 8-bit optimizers.
- Basic quantization uses `BitsAndBytesConfig` with `from_pretrained()`; 8-bit loading approximately halves memory usage.
- `device_map="auto"` distributes large models across available GPUs for inference, while CPU offloading and custom device maps provide more explicit placement.
- `llm_int8_threshold` controls outlier handling: the default is 6, while lower values can speed inference at the possible cost of accuracy.
- `llm_int8_skip_modules` can keep sensitive modules in full precision, such as BLOOM’s weight-shared `lm_head`.
- For 4-bit workflows, `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16` speeds computation, NF4 is recommended for training 4-bit base models, and double quantization saves another 0.4 bits per parameter.
- 8-bit and 4-bit training is limited to extra parameters, and dequantization can cause quality loss while requiring enough GPU memory for the restored model.

resources.title: [2203.02155] Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
resources.summary:
## Overview

This resource is the arXiv record for *Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback* (arXiv:2203.02155), a paper by Long Ouyang and 19 other authors, submitted on 4 March 2022. It is intended for readers interested in language-model alignment, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), and the InstructGPT models. The page provides the paper’s abstract and bibliographic information, establishing that human-feedback fine-tuning can make much smaller models preferable to larger GPT-3 models while improving truthfulness and reducing toxic output.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- Language-model alignment with user intent.
  - Alignment as the goal of making model outputs follow what users intend.
  - The distinction between model scale and the ability to follow instructions.
  - Failure modes identified in the abstract:
    - Untruthful outputs.
    - Toxic outputs.
    - Outputs that are not helpful to users.
- Supervised fine-tuning.
  - Collection of labeler-written demonstrations of desirable model behavior.
  - Starting prompts from:
    - Labeler-written prompts.
    - Prompts submitted through the OpenAI API.
  - Use of demonstrations to fine-tune GPT-3.
- Reinforcement learning from human feedback.
  - Collection of rankings of model outputs.
  - Further fine-tuning of the supervised model using human-ranked outputs.
  - Training signal derived from human preferences rather than demonstrations alone.
- InstructGPT.
  - Name given to the models produced through the described alignment procedure.
  - Models obtained by combining supervised fine-tuning and subsequent RLHF.
- Prompt distribution.
  - Human evaluations performed on the authors’ prompt distribution.
  - Comparison of model outputs based on human preference.
- Parameter-count comparison.
  - InstructGPT model with 1.3 billion parameters.
  - GPT-3 model with 175 billion parameters.
  - Reported comparison between the 1.3B and 175B models.
- Human evaluation of output quality.
  - Preference judgments comparing generated outputs.
  - Evaluation of helpfulness and adherence to user intent through human judgments.
- Truthfulness.
  - Reported improvement in truthfulness for InstructGPT models.
- Toxic output generation.
  - Reported reduction in toxic output generation.
- Public NLP benchmarks.
  - Minimal performance regressions on public NLP datasets.
- Human feedback data collection.
  - Labeler demonstrations of desired behavior.
  - Rankings of model outputs.
- Research context and metadata.
  - arXiv identifier: `2203.02155`.
  - arXiv category: Computer Science > Computation and Language.
  - Additional subject classifications:
    - Artificial Intelligence (`cs.AI`).
    - Machine Learning (`cs.LG`).
  - Submission date: 4 March 2022.
  - DOI: `10.48550/arXiv.2203.02155`.
  - Versioned citation: `arXiv:2203.02155v1 [cs.CL]`.
  - Full-text links to PDF, experimental HTML, and TeX source.

## Detailed Notes

**Resource identity and publication information**

The page is the arXiv record for *Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback*. It identifies the work as arXiv:2203.02155, submitted on 4 March 2022. The listed subject area is Computation and Language (`cs.CL`), with Artificial Intelligence (`cs.AI`) and Machine Learning (`cs.LG`) also shown as related subject classifications. The record lists Long Ouyang, Jeff Wu, Xu Jiang, Diogo Almeida, Carroll L. Wainwright, Pamela Mishkin, Chong Zhang, Sandhini Agarwal, Katarina Slama, Alex Ray, John Schulman, Jacob Hilton, Fraser Kelton, Luke Miller, Maddie Simens, Amanda Askell, Peter Welinder, Paul Christiano, Jan Leike, and Ryan Lowe as authors.

The page provides links to the PDF, an experimental HTML version, and the TeX source. The cited DOI is `10.48550/arXiv.2203.02155`. The page also supports citation in arXiv form as `arXiv:2203.02155 [cs.CL]` or `arXiv:2203.02155v1 [cs.CL]` for the displayed version.

**Motivation: scale is not equivalent to instruction following**

The paper begins from the observation that making language models larger does not inherently improve their ability to follow a user’s intent. The abstract gives concrete examples of undesirable behavior from large language models:

- Producing untruthful outputs.
- Producing toxic outputs.
- Producing outputs that are simply not helpful to the user.

These behaviors are described as evidence that the models are not aligned with their users. The paper therefore frames alignment, rather than parameter count alone, as the central problem to address.

**Supervised fine-tuning stage**

The proposed alignment process starts by collecting prompts from two sources:

1. Prompts written by labelers.
2. Prompts submitted through the OpenAI API.

For these prompts, the authors collect a dataset of demonstrations written by labelers. These demonstrations represent desired model behavior. The demonstration dataset is then used to fine-tune GPT-3 through supervised learning.

The supervised stage therefore provides the initial instruction-following adjustment to GPT-3. The page describes the data source and training modality, but the extracted text does not provide the number of prompts, demonstrations, model configuration, learning rate, batch size, or other implementation details.

**Reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback stage**

After supervised fine-tuning, the authors collect a dataset consisting of rankings of model outputs. These rankings provide a preference signal for comparing outputs.

The supervised model is then further fine-tuned using reinforcement learning from human feedback. In the procedure summarized by the abstract, the process is therefore:

1. Collect labeler-written and OpenAI API-submitted prompts.
2. Collect demonstrations of desirable behavior.
3. Fine-tune GPT-3 with supervised learning.
4. Collect rankings of model outputs.
5. Further fine-tune the supervised model with RLHF.

The page does not state the exact RL algorithm, reward-model architecture, optimization procedure, or training hyperparameters. It explicitly identifies the human rankings as the feedback used for the reinforcement-learning stage.

**InstructGPT models**

The resulting models are called **InstructGPT**. The name applies to the models produced by the described procedure, which combines supervised fine-tuning with a subsequent human-feedback reinforcement-learning stage.

The abstract does not list all model sizes, but it specifically reports a 1.3-billion-parameter InstructGPT model. It compares this model with a 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 model.

**Human preference evaluation**

The main comparative evaluation described in the abstract uses human evaluations over the authors’ prompt distribution. The reported result is that outputs from the **1.3B-parameter InstructGPT** model are preferred to outputs from the **175B-parameter GPT-3** model.

This comparison is important because the preferred InstructGPT model has 100 times fewer parameters than the GPT-3 model used for comparison. The result supports the paper’s central claim that human-feedback fine-tuning can improve alignment-related behavior without requiring the largest available model.

The page does not provide:

- The number of evaluators.
- The number of evaluation prompts.
- The preference percentages or statistical significance values.
- The comparison protocol.
- The exact task categories used in the evaluation.

**Truthfulness and toxicity**

The abstract reports two additional behavioral effects for InstructGPT:

- Improvements in truthfulness.
- Reductions in toxic output generation.

These results are presented as evidence that fine-tuning with human feedback improves behavior beyond simply increasing model size. The extracted page does not define the truthfulness or toxicity metrics, describe the datasets used to measure them, or provide numerical effect sizes.

**Performance on public NLP datasets**

The authors report **minimal performance regressions on public NLP datasets** for InstructGPT models. This indicates that the alignment-oriented fine-tuning does not, according to the abstract, cause a large degradation on the public NLP evaluations considered by the authors.

The page does not identify the individual public datasets, metrics, baseline scores, or regression sizes.

**Limitations stated or implied by the page**

The abstract explicitly states that InstructGPT still makes simple mistakes. Thus, the method is presented as a promising alignment direction rather than a complete solution to language-model reliability.

The page also makes clear that the behavioral claims are evaluated in the context of the authors’ prompt distribution. It does not establish, on the basis of the extracted text alone, how the models perform on every possible task or distribution. Other implementation details, data scales, reward-model details, and evaluation statistics are not present in the supplied page text.

## Key Concepts & References

- **Language-model alignment:** Aligning model behavior with user intent.
- **User intent:** The intended purpose or desired result of a user’s prompt.
- **GPT-3:** The base language model fine-tuned in the described procedure.
- **Supervised fine-tuning:** Training a model using demonstrations of desired outputs.
- **Labeler demonstrations:** Human-written examples of preferred model behavior.
- **OpenAI API prompts:** Prompts submitted through the OpenAI API and used as part of the data collection process.
- **Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF):** Further model training based on human feedback, here expressed through rankings of outputs.
- **Output ranking:** A comparative preference signal obtained by ranking model outputs.
- **InstructGPT:** The resulting models after supervised fine-tuning and human-feedback reinforcement learning.
- **Human evaluation:** Evaluation of generated outputs through human preferences on the authors’ prompt distribution.
- **1.3B-parameter model:** The smaller InstructGPT model reported to outperform a 175B-parameter GPT-3 model in preference evaluations.
- **175B-parameter GPT-3:** The larger comparison model in the reported human evaluation.
- **Truthfulness:** A behavioral quality reported to improve for InstructGPT.
- **Toxic output generation:** A behavioral problem reported to decrease for InstructGPT.
- **Public NLP datasets:** Evaluation resources on which minimal performance regressions were observed.
- **arXiv:2203.02155:** The paper’s arXiv identifier.
- **DOI `10.48550/arXiv.2203.02155`:** The arXiv-issued DOI listed on the page.

## Takeaways

- The paper argues that model size alone does not ensure that a language model follows a user’s intent.
- Its alignment pipeline begins with supervised fine-tuning of GPT-3 using labeler demonstrations of desirable behavior.
- It then applies reinforcement learning from human feedback using human rankings of model outputs.
- The resulting models are called InstructGPT.
- On the authors’ prompt distribution, a 1.3B-parameter InstructGPT model is reported to produce outputs preferred to those of a 175B-parameter GPT-3 model.
- The abstract reports improved truthfulness and reduced toxic output generation, with minimal regressions on public NLP datasets.
- InstructGPT still makes simple mistakes, so human-feedback fine-tuning is presented as a promising direction rather than a complete solution.

resources.title: [2305.18290] Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
resources.summary:
## Overview

This arXiv paper introduces **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)**, a method for aligning language models with human preferences without the conventional two-stage reward-model-and-reinforcement-learning pipeline. It is intended for researchers and practitioners working on language-model alignment, preference optimization, and RLHF; the page presents the paper’s abstract, publication history, and links to its PDF and experimental HTML version.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- **Unsupervised language-model training**
  - Large language models learn broad world knowledge through unsupervised training.
  - Some reasoning skills can emerge from large-scale unsupervised training.
  - Precise behavioral control remains difficult because the training signal is unsupervised.

- **Language-model steerability**
  - Controlling the behavior of a pretrained language model.
  - Aligning generated responses with human preferences.
  - Controlling attributes such as the sentiment of generated text.

- **Human preference labels**
  - Collecting labels that compare the relative quality of different model generations.
  - Using preferred and dispreferred generations as alignment data.

- **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)**
  - Conventional use of human preference feedback to fine-tune an unsupervised language model.
  - Reward-model fitting as the first stage.
  - Reinforcement-learning-based policy optimization as the second stage.
  - Avoiding excessive drift from the original language model.
  - The described limitations of RLHF: complexity and instability.

- **Reward modeling**
  - Fitting a reward model that estimates human preferences.
  - Rewriting the reward-model parameterization so that its optimal policy can be recovered in closed form.

- **Policy extraction in closed form**
  - Deriving the policy corresponding to the reparameterized reward model.
  - Replacing an explicit reinforcement-learning optimization process with direct optimization through a loss function.

- **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)**
  - The paper’s new alignment algorithm.
  - Optimization using a simple classification loss.
  - Direct preference-based fine-tuning of the language model.
  - Avoiding sampling from the language model during fine-tuning.
  - Avoiding substantial hyperparameter tuning.
  - Reported stability, performance, and computational lightweightness.

- **PPO-based RLHF**
  - Proximal Policy Optimization as an existing reinforcement-learning method used in RLHF.
  - Comparison of DPO with PPO-based RLHF.
  - DPO’s reported advantage in sentiment control.
  - DPO’s reported equal or improved performance in summarization and single-turn dialogue.

- **Empirical evaluation domains**
  - Sentiment-controlled generation.
  - Summarization.
  - Single-turn dialogue.

- **Resource and publication metadata**
  - arXiv identifier: **2305.18290**.
  - Initial submission on **29 May 2023**.
  - Second version on **13 December 2023**.
  - Third and current version on **29 July 2024**.
  - PDF access.
  - Experimental HTML access.
  - Authorship attributed to **Rafael Rafailov and five other authors**.

## Detailed Notes

### Problem setting

The paper begins from the observation that large-scale unsupervised language models can acquire broad world knowledge and some reasoning ability, but their behavior is difficult to control precisely. The page attributes this difficulty to the “completely unsupervised nature” of their training.

A common alignment approach collects **human labels comparing the relative quality of model generations**. These labels are then used to fine-tune the unsupervised language model so that it generates outputs preferred by humans.

### Conventional RLHF pipeline

The page describes standard RLHF as a complex and potentially unstable procedure with two principal stages:

1. **Fit a reward model** to reflect human preferences.
2. **Fine-tune the language model with reinforcement learning** to maximize the estimated reward while avoiding excessive drift from the original model.

Thus, conventional RLHF introduces both a separate reward-fitting stage and a reinforcement-learning optimization stage. The paper’s proposed method is designed to simplify this pipeline.

### DPO reward-model parameterization

The central technical contribution is a **new parameterization of the reward model used in RLHF**. Under this parameterization, the corresponding optimal policy can be extracted **in closed form**.

The page does not provide the mathematical derivation, equations, notation, or exact parameterization from the abstract. It nevertheless emphasizes that closed-form policy extraction is what permits the standard RLHF objective to be solved using a simple classification loss rather than an explicit reinforcement-learning procedure.

### Direct Preference Optimization

The resulting algorithm is named **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)**. According to the abstract, DPO:

- Fine-tunes a language model directly from preference feedback.
- Uses a **simple classification loss**.
- Eliminates the need to sample from the language model during fine-tuning.
- Eliminates the need for substantial hyperparameter tuning.
- Is described as stable, performant, and computationally lightweight.
- Avoids the conventional sequence of fitting a separate reward model and then optimizing the language model through reinforcement learning.

The page does not specify the exact loss formula, dataset construction procedure, model architectures, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, regularization settings, or implementation API.

### Experimental claims

The abstract reports that DPO can align language models with human preferences as well as or better than existing methods. Specifically:

- **Sentiment control:** DPO exceeds PPO-based RLHF in its ability to control the sentiment of generations.
- **Summarization:** DPO matches or improves response quality relative to the compared methods.
- **Single-turn dialogue:** DPO matches or improves response quality relative to the compared methods.
- **Practicality:** DPO is substantially simpler to implement and train.

These are claims reported in the abstract; the supplied page text does not include experimental tables, baselines beyond PPO-based RLHF, numerical results, dataset names, or statistical analyses.

### Availability and version history

The resource is available through:

- A **PDF** of the paper.
- An **experimental HTML** rendering.
- A version history showing the initial submission and two later revisions.

The arXiv metadata records:

- **v1:** 29 May 2023.
- **v2:** 13 December 2023.
- **v3:** 29 July 2024, identified as the current version on the page.

The paper is titled *Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model* and is listed under arXiv identifier **2305.18290**.

## Key Concepts & References

- **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO)** — the paper’s proposed preference-alignment algorithm.
- **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)** — the conventional alignment framework being simplified.
- **PPO-based RLHF** — the reinforcement-learning baseline used in the comparison.
- **Reward model** — a model fitted to estimate human preferences.
- **Closed-form optimal policy** — the policy recovered from DPO’s reward-model parameterization.
- **Classification loss** — the simple loss used to optimize DPO.
- **Human preference alignment** — fine-tuning generated responses according to preferred versus dispreferred outputs.
- **Sentiment control** — one of the reported evaluation capabilities.
- **Summarization** — one of the reported evaluation tasks.
- **Single-turn dialogue** — one of the reported evaluation tasks.
- **arXiv:2305.18290** — the paper’s reference identifier.

## Takeaways

- DPO replaces the conventional RLHF sequence of reward-model training followed by reinforcement-learning optimization with direct preference optimization.
- Its key technical device is a reward-model parameterization that allows the optimal policy to be extracted in closed form.
- Training uses a simple classification loss rather than the standard RLHF reinforcement-learning procedure.
- The abstract reports that DPO removes language-model sampling during fine-tuning and substantially reduces hyperparameter tuning.
- Experiments report stronger sentiment control than PPO-based RLHF and equal or better summarization and single-turn-dialogue quality.
- The supplied page is an abstract and metadata record, so it does not include the derivation, equations, implementation details, or numerical experiments.

resources.title: [2402.14740] Back to Basics: Revisiting REINFORCE Style Optimization for Learning from Human Feedback in LLMs
resources.summary:
## Overview

This resource is the arXiv page for *Back to Basics: Revisiting REINFORCE Style Optimization for Learning from Human Feedback in LLMs*, a paper by Arash Ahmadian and seven other authors. It is aimed at readers working on RLHF and alignment for large language models, presenting the argument that carefully adapted, simpler REINFORCE-style optimization can match or improve on more computationally expensive and sensitive methods, including PPO, DPO, and RAFT.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- AI alignment for large language models through Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).
- The role of RL in the RLHF pipeline.
- Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) as a commonly used method for the RL component of RLHF.
- Computational cost associated with PPO-based RLHF.
- Hyperparameter sensitivity associated with PPO.
- The motivations that originally led to the development of PPO.
- The claim that PPO’s motivating concerns are less practically important in the RLHF setting.
- Re-examination of preference-based alignment as a reinforcement learning problem.
- REINFORCE-style optimization as a simpler alternative for RLHF.
- Adaptation of reinforcement learning methods to the characteristics of LLM alignment.
- Comparison with PPO.
- Comparison with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), described in the abstract as an “RL-free” method.
- Comparison with RAFT, also described in the abstract as an “RL-free” method.
- The reported finding that simpler REINFORCE-style variants outperform both PPO and newer “RL-free” alternatives.
- The proposal that online reinforcement learning optimization can be beneficial at low computational cost for LLM alignment.
- The paper’s guiding principle of keeping the optimization method simple.
- Availability of the paper as a PDF.
- Experimental availability of an HTML version.
- Submission and revision metadata:
  - Initial submission: 22 February 2024.
  - Revised version: 26 February 2024.
  - The page identifies the revised version as version 2.
  - Version 1 is listed as 204 KB.
  - Version 2 is listed as 205 KB.

## Detailed Notes

### Problem context

The paper begins from the position that AI alignment expressed through RLHF has become an important ingredient in producing high-performance large language models.

RLHF is treated as an alignment framework in which human preferences provide the learning signal. The paper focuses specifically on the reinforcement learning stage of this process rather than presenting a general survey of all components of RLHF.

### PPO as the conventional RLHF method

The abstract identifies Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO, as the method that recent literature has positioned as canonical for the RL part of RLHF.

Two practical limitations are emphasized:

- PPO has a high computational cost.
- PPO requires sensitive hyperparameter tuning.

The paper questions whether the design principles that motivated PPO remain equally important when the method is applied to RLHF for large language models.

### Central research hypothesis

The authors posit that many of the motivational principles behind PPO are less of a practical concern in an RLHF context.

Their proposed direction is therefore not simply to improve PPO, but to revisit the underlying alignment formulation and seek a less computationally expensive optimization method that can preserve or increase performance.

### REINFORCE-style optimization

The paper advocates a return to REINFORCE-style optimization, adapted carefully to the characteristics of LLM alignment.

The stated design principle is simplicity. The abstract claims that many PPO components are unnecessary in this setting and that simpler REINFORCE-style variants can produce better results.

## Overview

DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale is a research paper and open-source system focused on making large-scale reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models more reproducible. It presents the Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization (DAPO) algorithm, reports a 50-point score on AIME 2024 with the Qwen2.5-32B base model, and makes the training code and curated dataset publicly available through a system built on the `verl` framework. The resource is aimed at researchers and practitioners working on reasoning-oriented LLM training and large-scale RL systems.

## Syllabus / Topics Covered

- Large language model reasoning
  - Inference scaling and its role in improving LLM reasoning
  - Reinforcement learning as a technique for eliciting complex reasoning
  - Reproducibility challenges in RL training for state-of-the-art reasoning LLMs
- DAPO algorithm
  - Full name: Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization
  - The paper’s claim that DAPO introduces four key techniques supporting large-scale LLM RL
  - The extracted page does not enumerate or explain the four techniques
- Open-source large-scale RL system
  - Fully open-sourced system for large-scale LLM reinforcement learning
  - Training code
  - Carefully curated and processed dataset
  - Reproducibility and support for future research
- Model and benchmark evaluation
  - Qwen2.5-32B as the base model
  - AIME 2024 as the reported benchmark
  - Reported result: 50 points on AIME 2024
- Software infrastructure
  - Training implementation built on the `verl` framework
  - Relationship between the DAPO algorithm and the open-source training system
- Research context and related work
  - OpenAI o1 blog as an example of concealed state-of-the-art reasoning-LLM training details
  - DeepSeek R1 technical report as another example
  - Community difficulty in reproducing RL training results from partially disclosed systems
- Publication information
  - arXiv identifier: `[2503.14476]`
  - Initial submission: 18 March 2025
  - Version 2 revision: 20 May 2025
  - Author list includes Qiying Yu, Zheng Zhang, Ruofei Zhu, Yufeng Yuan, Xiaochen Zuo, and additional collaborators

## Detailed Notes

### Motivation and research problem

The paper begins from the observation that inference scaling has enabled large language models to demonstrate substantial reasoning ability. It identifies reinforcement learning as a core technique for eliciting complex reasoning.

The motivation is reproducibility. The authors argue that important technical details of state-of-the-art reasoning LLMs have been withheld, citing the OpenAI o1 blog and the DeepSeek R1 technical report as examples. As a result, the community has difficulty reproducing the RL training results of these systems.

### DAPO

The paper introduces the **Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization** algorithm, abbreviated as **DAPO**.

The abstract states that DAPO includes four key techniques that the authors believe make large-scale LLM reinforcement learning successful. However, the extracted page text does not name those four techniques or provide their algorithms, equations, implementation details, or ablations. Therefore, the specific meanings of the “decoupled clip” and “dynamic sampling” components cannot be reconstructed from the supplied page text alone.

### Reported system and result

The authors describe DAPO as part of a fully open-source, state-of-the-art large-scale reinforcement learning system. According to the abstract, the system:

- Uses **Qwen2.5-32B** as its base model.
- Achieves **50 points on AIME 2024**.
- Includes open-source training code.
- Includes a carefully curated and processed dataset.
- Is intended to improve reproducibility and support future research in large-scale LLM RL.

The supplied page text does not specify:

- The exact AIME 2024 evaluation protocol.
- Whether the 50-point result is a score, percentage, or another reported metric beyond the wording “50 points.”
- The number of training steps, rollout count, hardware, or computational budget.
- The complete model configuration or training hyperparameters.
- The precise data sources, dataset size, filtering rules, or preprocessing procedure.

### Software implementation

The open-source training code is built on the **`verl` framework**.

The page identifies `verl` as the implementation foundation but does not provide:

- Installation commands.
- API signatures.
- Configuration files.
- Training launch commands.
- Dependency versions.
- Distributed-training settings.
- Rollout, reward, or optimizer interfaces.

The only implementation-level fact available in the extracted text is that the authors’ training code is built on `verl`.

### Dataset release

The authors also release or make available a carefully curated and processed dataset. The supplied text does not describe the dataset beyond that characterization. It provides no information about its:

- Name.
- Size.
- Source domains.
- Mathematical-problem composition.
- Formatting.
- Train/validation split.
- Filtering criteria.
- Processing pipeline.
- Licensing or access instructions.

### Reproducibility and open-source components

The abstract presents the combination of the DAPO algorithm, training code, and processed dataset as the main contribution to reproducibility. The intended benefit is that researchers can examine and build on a large-scale LLM RL system rather than relying only on high-level descriptions or selectively disclosed details.

The paper contrasts this approach with prior works that withhold key training details. The comparison is general; the extracted page does not provide a side-by-side comparison with OpenAI o1, DeepSeek R1, or other systems.

### Publication and version information

The resource is identified as arXiv paper `[2503.14476]`, titled **DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale**.

- Version 1 was submitted on 18 March 2025 at 17:49:06 UTC.
- Version 2 was submitted on 20 May 2025 at 01:37:34 UTC.

## Key Concepts & References

- **DAPO** — Decoupled Clip and Dynamic Sampling Policy Optimization.

## Takeaways

- DAPO proposes a large-scale LLM reinforcement learning algorithm and an open-source system for training reasoning models.
- The system is built on the `verl` framework and includes both training code and a curated, processed dataset.
- Using Qwen2.5-32B, the authors report a score of 50 points on AIME 2024.
- The paper’s main motivation is to make large-scale reasoning-LLM RL training more reproducible when important details are otherwise withheld.
- The abstract claims that DAPO introduces four key techniques, but the supplied page text does not identify them.

## Overview

This intermediate lecture presents a from-scratch PyTorch implementation of Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for finetuning a roughly 135-million-parameter language model to generate explicit reasoning followed by a verified final answer. - [ ] Definition of GRPO as **Group Relative Policy Optimization**.

### Task environment and dataset construction

### Prompting, answer extraction, and evaluation

- [ ] System prompt requiring reasoning inside `<think>` tags.

- [ ] XML-like target response format:
  - [ ] `<think>` opening tag.

  - [ ] Call `client.chat.completions.create(...)`.

### GRPO’s two phases

- [ ] Experience-collection phase.
- [ ] Training phase.

### Experience collection

- [ ] Sampling a batch of questions.

### Group-relative advantages

- [ ] Grouping responses by the original question.

### Policy-gradient objective

- [ ] Simplified objective over responses and tokens.
- [ ] Maximization of the policy-gradient objective.
- [ ] Mean over the group through \(1/G\).
- [ ] Mean over output tokens through \(1/|o_i|\).

- [ ] Autoregressive dependence on preceding generated tokens.
- [ ] Assignment of one response-level advantage to every generated token.
- [ ] Consequence for positive advantages: increase generated-token probabilities.
- [ ] Consequence for negative advantages: decrease generated-token probabilities.
- [ ] Assumption that all generated tokens are equally responsible for the outcome.
- [ ] Important source caveat: the lecture notes are internally inconsistent about the exact policy-gradient notation.

### Positive and negative advantages

- [ ] Comparison of high-scoring `ABC` with advantage \(+1\).

- [ ] Policy probabilities change; advantages do not.

- [ ] Equivalent log-probability interpretation:
  - [ ] Increase positive-advantage token log probabilities.
  - [ ] Decrease negative-advantage token log probabilities.

### Importance sampling

- [ ] Importance-sampling ratio between current and old policies:
  \[
  r_{i,t}(\theta)=
  \frac{\pi_\theta(o_{i,t}\mid q_i,o_{i,<t})}
  {\pi_{\text{old}}(o_{i,t}\mid q_i,o_{i,<t})}
  \]
- [ ] Definition of \(\pi_{\text{old}}\) as the experience-collection policy.
- [ ] Definition of \(\pi_\theta\) as the policy currently being updated.
- [ ] Old-policy log probabilities stored during generation.
- [ ] Current-policy probabilities computed from updated weights.
- [ ] Ratio as a measure of policy change.
- [ ] Reweighting of advantages according to current-versus-old behavior.

### PPO-style clipping and GRPO loss

- [ ] PPO-style clipping of the importance ratio.
- [ ] Clipped ratio:
  \[
  \operatorname{clip}\left(r_{i,t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)
  \]
- [ ] Example clipping parameter \(\epsilon=0.2\).
- [ ] Corresponding ratio range:
  \[
  0.8\le r_{i,t}(\theta)\le1.2
  \]
- [ ] Clipping as a regularizing mechanism.
- [ ] Prevention of:
  - [ ] Very large policy updates.
  - [ ] Rapid weight changes.
  - [ ] Excessive token-probability changes.
  - [ ] Unstable training.
- [ ] Graded policy-update principle: move useful token probabilities in the correct direction without moving too far in one update.
- [ ] PPO-style minimum of clipped and unclipped objectives.
- [ ] Negative GRPO loss:
  \[
  \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=
  -\frac1G\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac1{|o_i|}
  \sum_{t=1}^{|o_i|}
  \min\left[
  r_{i,t}(\theta)A_{i,t},
  \operatorname{clip}\left(r_{i,t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)A_{i,t}
  \right]
  \]
- [ ] Maximizing the corresponding objective is equivalent to minimizing this negative loss.

### Coding experience collection
